Java did copy. It copied the arrow. The method got its own variable called account, holding a second arrow to the same object, exactly like backup earlier. Two arrows, one account, so the fee lands on the real thing.

A method parameter holding a second reference to the same objectTwo boxes on the left represent variables in different places: ada in the main method and account inside applyFee. Both have arrows pointing at the same Account object on the right, which is why a change made inside the method is visible outside it.in maininside applyFeeadaaccountAccount495.00The arrow was copied. The account was not.

There is a real limit to this, and it is worth seeing once.

public static void replace(Account account) {
    account = new Account("AC-9999", "Nobody", 0.00);
}

Call that with ada and ada is unchanged. The method pointed its own arrow somewhere else. The caller's arrow never moved. You can change the object a method was handed. You cannot change which object the caller is looking at.

If you remember one thing. A variable never holds an object. It holds the way to reach one, and several variables can hold the way to reach the same one.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
Predict first, then run

Write this in main. Before you run it, write down on paper what each of the four lines will print.

Account ada    = new Account("AC-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 500.00);
Account backup = ada;
Account twin   = new Account("AC-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 500.00);

backup.withdraw(200.00);

System.out.println(ada.getBalance());     // 1
System.out.println(twin.getBalance());    // 2
System.out.println(ada == backup);        // 3
System.out.println(ada == twin);          // 4

Now run it. For every line you got wrong, do not just accept the answer. Draw the boxes and arrows on paper until the picture explains the output, then check your drawing against the first diagram on this page.

Then one more, which is the one that matters:

Account nothing = null;
System.out.println(nothing == null);       // fine
System.out.println(nothing.getBalance());  // not fine

Run it and read the exception message properly, all of it. You will meet this message more often than any other in Java, and being able to read it is a skill worth ten minutes now.

docs.title: Think about it
docs.text:
1. backup = ada copies an arrow rather than the account. Suppose you genuinely wanted a separate account with the same values. You cannot get it from an assignment. What would you have to do instead, and what would you have to decide along the way?

  2. == compares arrows, which means two accounts with the same number are not equal. For a bank, is that the right default or the wrong one? Argue it, then consider a system where the same customer record is loaded twice from a file.

  3. A method can change the object you handed it but cannot change which object you are looking at. Is that a sensible rule or an accident of how Java works? Think about what the alternative would let a method do to your variables.

  4. Nobody points an arrow at the object made inside replace once the method ends. What happens to it? You have not been taught the answer. Work out what must happen, and what would go wrong if it did not.

Week 3, session 1. Objects that refuse

docs.title: Seminar 1. Setting up and designing
docs.text:
2 hoursWeek 1 seminarFollows: Thinking in things, Why objects

By the end of this session your machine compiles and runs Java, your work is in a repository on GitHub, and you have designed the university system on paper. You write no Java today.

Two jobs, and the first one is not optional. If you leave without a working toolchain, week 2 is a wasted lecture for you and a slow one for everyone who has to wait.

How the two hours are dividedA horizontal bar split into three parts: sixty minutes setting up the machine, fifty minutes designing on paper, and ten minutes committing the work.Set up the machineDesign on paper60 min50 min10Push

docs.title: Part 1. Get your machine working
docs.text:
Sixty minutes, on your own. Work through the four setup pages in order and do not skip ahead.

  1. Install Java — Temurin 25, then verify it from a terminal.
  2. Install Eclipse — including the checksum step.
  3. Git and GitHub — your own repository, your first push.

Each page has a troubleshooting section with the exact error messages you are likely to see. Read the message, find it on the page, then ask.

Not in OneDrive, Desktop or Documents

Those folders sync to the cloud, and the sync client rewrites files while the compiler is reading them. The result is not a clear error. It is builds that fail then succeed, files that revert while you are editing, and eventually a git repository that corrupts itself.

Put your workspace at C:\dev\workspace and your repository at C:\dev\. This costs you nothing now and saves you a weekend in week nine.

You are through part 1 when all four of these are true

In a fresh PowerShell window:

java -version      # reports 25
javac -version     # reports 25
git --version      # reports something

And on github.com, your repository exists and contains at least one commit that you pushed from this machine.

If any of those is missing, stay on part 1. Part 2 needs the repository.

docs.title: Part 2. Design before you code
docs.text:
Fifty minutes. Paper and pen. Close the laptop.

Read the scenario at the top of the university system and stop there. Do not scroll down to the class specifications. The whole value of this exercise is that you work it out first.

docs.title: Task 1. Find the things
docs.text:
List what you think should be classes. Aim for three to five, not ten.

For each one, write a single sentence saying why it earns a class, using the three questions from the lecture: does it have data of its own that must stay correct, are there rules about that data, and can you ask it to do something.

docs.title: Task 2. What each one knows
docs.text:
Under each class, list the data it owns. Beside each piece of data, write whether it can ever change after the object is created.

That second column is doing more work than it looks. It is the difference between a field and a fixed field, and week 3 turns it into a final keyword.

docs.title: Task 3. What each one does, including one refusal
docs.text:
Under each class, list what you can ask it to do.

Then the part that matters: for each class, write one thing it can refuse, and say what it needs to know in order to refuse it. A class that can only hand over its data is a container. A class that can say no is an object.

If one of your classes has nothing it can refuse, look again. Either you missed a rule in the scenario, or that thing is not really a class.

docs.title: Task 4. Who asks whom
docs.text:
Write three sentences describing what happens when a student enrols in a course. Use only this shape:

X asks Y to ...

No sentence may say that one thing reaches into another and changes its data. If you cannot write it without doing that, you have found a place where a rule lives in the wrong class.

docs.title: Task 5. Two nouns that are not classes
docs.text:
The scenario contains nouns that should not become classes. Find two of them and write one sentence each saying why.

This is the exam question you will see in some form, and it is the one most people get wrong, because underlining nouns is easy and thinking about them is not.

docs.title: Task 6. Compare
docs.text:
Now open the class specifications on the university system page.

For every place you differ, write one line: what you had, what is there, and whether you would defend your version.

Some of your answers will be better. Enrolment is a perfectly reasonable class that the specification does not have. A different set of rules on Course may well be the right call. The comparison is the lesson, not the correction. From week 2 onward you use the specification's names, so that everyone's code can be talked about, but that is a convention, not a verdict on your design.

docs.title: Part 3. Commit your design
docs.text:
Ten minutes. Your design is work, so it belongs in the repository like everything else.

Type your notes into a file called design.md in your repository. Keep it rough. Bullet points are fine.

## Student
knows:  studentId (never changes), name, gpa, enrolmentYear (never changes)
does:   register for a course, update gpa, report academic standing
refuses: registering for a seventh course
        needs to know: how many courses it already has

## Not classes
Enrolment year - a number that belongs to a student
Teaching load  - counted from the courses a professor has

Then:

cd C:\dev\java-oop-yourname
git add design.md
git commit -m "Week 1: university system design"
git push

Refresh GitHub and check it is there. That is your second commit and your first piece of real work under version control.

docs.title: Before you leave
docs.text:
• java -version and javac -version both report 25
  • Eclipse opens and runs a class
  • Your repository exists on GitHub with your name on it
  • design.md is pushed and visible in the browser
  • You have written down at least one place where your design differs from the specification

If the first four are done, week 2 will work for you. If any are missing, finish them before the next lecture rather than during it.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
Only if you are done and have time left.

Design something else. Take a system you actually use, a food delivery app or a library or the university's own portal, and run tasks 1 to 5 on it in ten minutes. There is no specification to compare against, which is closer to real work.

Find the hard rule. In the scenario, "a course cannot be scheduled into a room too small for the students enrolled in it" involves three things at once. Work out which one should enforce it and what it needs to know. There is more than one defensible answer and you will meet this again in week 6.

Set up your editor properly. Turn on line numbers in Eclipse, and learn three shortcuts: Ctrl+Shift+T to open any class, Alt+Shift+R to rename, Ctrl+Shift+F to format. You will use them several hundred times this semester.

Week 2, session 1. Your first class

docs.title: Seminar 2. Your first classes
docs.text:
2 hoursWeek 2 seminarFollows: Your first class, What a variable really holds

By the end of this session you have three working Java classes from the design you made last week, and you can predict what happens when two variables refer to the same object.

No validation today. Your constructors will accept anything you hand them, including nonsense, and that is deliberate. Next week is about making them refuse. Write the classes first, feel where the holes are, then close them.

How the two hours are dividedA horizontal bar split into four parts: twenty minutes on a warm-up class, sixty minutes on the three main classes, twenty minutes on a references drill, and ten minutes to commit.Warm-upThree classesDrill2060 min2010

docs.title: Warm-up. Classroom
docs.text:
Twenty minutes. Build Classroom from the specification. It is the simplest of the five, and it exercises everything you will need for the next hour.

Four fields, one constructor, getters, three behaviour methods, toString.

Two things to get right, because you will repeat them fifteen times today:

roomNumber and building have getters and no setters. A room does not move to another building. hasProjector has a setter, because equipment does change.

location() returns text, it does not print it. Same for toString. Nothing in this class calls System.out.println.

When it compiles, make two classrooms in a UniversityApp class with a main, print both, and call canAccommodate with a number that fits and one that does not.

If you are still fighting Eclipse at the twenty minute mark, stop and fix that first. Go back to the setup pages.

docs.title: Main task. Student, Professor, Course
docs.text:
Sixty minutes. These three are the system, and you extend them for the rest of the module.

Work through the specification one class at a time. Finish one completely before starting the next, because three half-written classes compile into nothing useful and you will not know which one is wrong.

For each class:

  1. Fields, all private.
  2. One constructor that takes everything the object needs. No empty constructor.
  3. Getters. Setters only where the specification says the value can change.
  4. The behaviour methods. These are the interesting part.
  5. toString(), with @Override above it.

docs.title: Where people lose time
docs.text:
The behaviour methods are the point, not the getters. academicStanding() and academicTitle() are where a class stops being a box of data. If you run short, write those before you write the last few getters.

this in the constructor. Leave it out and name = name assigns the parameter to itself. The compiler says nothing and your object prints a blank name.

Getter-only fields. studentId, employeeId and courseCode have no setters. If your fingers generated one out of habit, delete it.

One thing at a time. academicStanding() returns a String. It does not print, does not update the GPA, and does not check anything else.

Do not let Eclipse generate everything

Right-click, Source, Generate Getters and Setters is fast and it will produce a setter for every field, including the ones that must never change.

Use it if you like, then read every method it wrote and delete the ones that should not exist. Deleting them is the design work. The generator does the typing and you do the thinking.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
In UniversityApp.main, create two of each, print them all, and call every behaviour method at least once.

Student ada = new Student("S-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 3.9, 2024);
System.out.println(ada);
System.out.println(ada.academicStanding());

Expected shape, not exact wording: one readable line per object, and standings and titles that change when you change the numbers.

Try a student with a GPA of 1.2 and one with 3.5, and check the standing differs. If both say the same thing, your comparison chain is in the wrong order.

docs.title: Drill. Two names, one object
docs.text:
Twenty minutes, and do not skip it because you are behind. This catches a misconception that otherwise surfaces in week eleven, on a deadline.

Write each block, predict the output on paper first, then run it.

One

Student a = new Student("S-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 3.9, 2024);
Student b = a;
b.setName("Ada L.");
System.out.println(a.getName());

Two

Student x = new Student("S-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 3.9, 2024);
Student y = new Student("S-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 3.9, 2024);
System.out.println(x == y);
System.out.println(x.getStudentId() == y.getStudentId());
System.out.println(x.getStudentId().equals(y.getStudentId()));

Three

Student nobody = null;
System.out.println(nobody == null);
System.out.println(nobody.getName());

Four

public static void promote(Student student) {
    student.updateGpa(4.0);
}

public static void replace(Student student) {
    student = new Student("S-9999", "Nobody", 0.0, 2024);
}

Call both with the same student and print the GPA and name after each. One of them changes something and one does not.

For every prediction you got wrong, draw the boxes and arrows on paper until the picture explains the output. Check your drawing against the diagram on What a variable really holds.

Block two, line two is the one that catches almost everybody. Note down your answer and why.

docs.title: Commit
docs.text:
Ten minutes.

cd C:\dev\java-oop-yourname
git add .
git commit -m "Week 2: Student, Professor, Course and Classroom"
git push

Check on GitHub that the .java files are there and the bin folder is not. If bin appears, your .gitignore is missing or in the wrong folder. Fix it now, because by week four that folder is noise on every commit.

docs.title: Before you leave
docs.text:
• Four classes compile: Classroom, Student, Professor, Course
  • Every field is private
  • No class contains System.out.println
  • No setters on studentId, employeeId, courseCode, roomNumber or building
  • UniversityApp creates objects and prints them
  • All four drill blocks run, with your predictions written down
  • Pushed, and bin is not in the repository

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
Write Department. Three fields, and no relationships yet. Ten minutes.

Break your own constructor. Create a student with a GPA of 9.5, a negative year of experience, and a course with 200 credits. All of them work right now. Write down what each one lets through. That list is your task list for next week, written by you.

Two constructors, honestly. The specification says one constructor. Find a case where a second one would genuinely earn its place, not just save typing. Bring it to the lecture.

Week 3, lecture 1. Objects that refuse

docs.title: Seminar 3. Making them refuse
docs.text:
2 hoursWeek 3 seminarFollows: Objects that refuse, What belongs to whom

By the end of this session your three classes cannot be put into an invalid state, and you will have spent half an hour deliberately trying to break them.

Last week you wrote classes that accept anything. Today you close every hole you left, and then you go looking for the ones you missed. The second half is the part that teaches most.

How the two hours are dividedA horizontal bar split into four parts: fifteen minutes listing invariants on paper, fifty-five minutes hardening the classes, thirty minutes trying to break them, and ten minutes to commit.PaperHarden themBreak them1555 min30 min10

docs.title: Warm-up. The invariant list
docs.text:
Fifteen minutes. Paper, not Eclipse.

For each of your three classes, write every field down one column. Beside each field write the one thing that must always be true about it, from the moment the object exists until it is thrown away.

Student
  studentId       not blank, never changes after creation
  name            not blank
  gpa             between 0.0 and 4.0
  enrolmentYear   between 2000 and this year, never changes

Then a second pass. Beside each line, write where the rule has to be enforced. Some are the constructor only. Some are the constructor and a method. Some need no enforcement because the field can never change and the type already limits it.

That list is your task list for the next hour. Written by you, from your own code, which is why it will be more accurate than anything I could give you.

docs.title: Harden them
docs.text: Fifty-five minutes. Three passes over each class, in this order. Do not mix them, because doing all three at once on one class is how you end up with a file that does not compile and no idea which change broke it.

docs.title: Pass 1. Lock what never changes
docs.text:
Add final to every field your list says never changes. studentId, enrolmentYear, employeeId, courseCode.

Then compile. If the compiler complains, you have a setter you should not have or an assignment outside the constructor. Both are the compiler finding a design problem for you.

Delete any setter that now fails to compile. Do not work around it.

docs.title: Pass 2. Make the constructor a gate
docs.text:
Add the checks from your list. Bad data in, no object out.

if (gpa < 0.0 || gpa > 4.0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("GPA must be between 0 and 4: " + gpa);
}

Put the bad value in every message. "Invalid GPA" tells you nothing at 2am. "GPA must be between 0 and 4: 9.5" tells you where to look.

You will write the same "not blank" check in six places. That is a signal. Write it once as a private helper and call it from everywhere, as the lecture did with requireText. It takes no fields, so it should be static.

Then the methods that change things. updateGpa must enforce the same rule as the constructor, because an object that is born valid and can be made invalid afterwards was never protected at all.

docs.title: Pass 3. Audit the public surface
docs.text:
This is the pass people skip and it is the one that teaches design.

List every public method on each class. For each one, ask: is this something the thing genuinely does?

A student updates a GPA. A student does not have a GPA assigned by a stranger. A professor completes another year. A professor does not have their experience overwritten.

Delete the ones that fail. Deleting code you wrote last week is uncomfortable and it is the actual work. Make a note of each deletion for the checklist.

docs.title: Then: let them issue their own ids
docs.text:
Add a static counter to Student and Professor, as Account did in the lecture. The object produces its own identifier and the constructor no longer takes one.

private static int lastIdIssued = 1000;

Your constructor signature changes, which means UniversityApp changes too. That is expected. The specification describes what the object knows, not what the constructor asks for, and this is an improvement: nobody outside can pick an id, so nobody outside can pick one that is already taken.

Remember what this counter cannot do

It lives in memory. Close the program and it resets to 1000.

In week eleven you will save students to a file and load them back, and the next student you create will be handed an id that already belongs to somebody. That is not a bug in what you wrote today. It is the honest limit of a counter, and you should be able to say so out loud.

docs.title: Break them
docs.text:
Thirty minutes. The best half of the session.

Write a new class called BreakIt, with a main, whose only job is to put your objects into invalid states. Try everything you can think of.

new Student("", 3.9, 2024);
new Student("Ada", -1.0, 2024);
new Student("Ada", 3.9, 1850);
new Student(null, 3.9, 2024);
new Course("CS101", "Programming", 0, "Fall 2026");

Then the interesting ones, which are not about the constructor:

  • Create a valid student, then call every method that changes something with a bad value.
  • Create a valid professor, then call completeAnotherYear() two hundred times. Is there an upper limit? Should there be?
  • Set a name to a string of forty spaces. Does isBlank() catch that? Check.
  • Give a course a title of "" after construction, if you left a setter that allows it.

Score yourself. One point for every line that succeeds in creating or producing an invalid object. A perfect score is zero.

Then fix what you found, and run BreakIt again until it scores zero.

Working next to somebody

If there is somebody beside you, swap. Hand them your three classes and take theirs, then write BreakIt against code you did not write.

You will find more in theirs than you found in your own, and they will find more in yours. That is not a comment on either of you. It is the reason professional code is reviewed by somebody else, and it is worth experiencing three modules before you meet JUnit.

Keep BreakIt in the repository. It is the closest thing you have to a test suite until week ten, and in week ten you will convert it into one.

docs.title: Commit
docs.text:
Ten minutes.

git add .
git commit -m "Week 3: invariants enforced, ids generated, BreakIt scores zero"
git push

docs.title: Before you leave
docs.text:
• Every field that never changes is final
  • Every constructor refuses bad data with a message containing the bad value
  • Every method that changes a field enforces the same rule as the constructor
  • The "not blank" check exists once, as a static helper
  • Student and Professor issue their own ids
  • You deleted at least one method you wrote last week
  • BreakIt exists, is committed, and scores zero

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
An immutable class. Write Semester with a term and a year, both final, no setters, and a toString that returns "Fall 2026". Then replace the String semester field on Course with it. Notice that you can now hand a Semester to anything without wondering what it will do to it.

The rule you cannot enforce yet. "A student cannot register for more than six courses." Where does it belong, and what does that class need to know? It cannot know it yet. Write down what is missing. You add it next week.

A validation message somebody else can read. Your exception messages are written for you. Rewrite one of them for a user of a system who does not know your field names. Decide whether that is really the right place for such a message, and if not, whose job it is.

Week 4, lecture 1. Many objects

docs.title: Seminar 4. Connecting the system
docs.text:
2 hoursWeek 4 seminarFollows: Many objects, Objects that own other objects

By the end of this session your classes are connected: students hold courses, professors hold courses, and neither hands its list out to anybody. This is the last seminar of Module 1, and what you finish with is where Sprint 1 starts.

Three things get built today, and the third one is the one the whole module has been aiming at. A class that owns a collection is responsible for what happens to it, and a class that owns other objects asks them to work rather than reaching in.

How the two hours are dividedA horizontal bar split into four parts: fifteen minutes on a warm-up, sixty minutes building the relationships, twenty minutes trying to break them, and fifteen minutes to commit and read the sprint briefing.Warm-upConnect themBreakSprint1560 min2015

docs.title: Warm-up. Give a student a list
docs.text:
Fifteen minutes.

Add one field to Student:

private final List<Course> courses = new ArrayList<>();

Three deliberate choices in one line, and you should be able to say all three out loud.

private, so nobody outside can touch it. final, so the student always has exactly this list, even though what is in it changes. Created where it is declared, so there is no path through your code where a student exists without a list.

Then add getCourseCount(), which returns courses.size(), and print it for a new student. It should say zero, and your existing UniversityApp should still compile and run.

If Eclipse offers to import java.util.*, take the two specific imports instead. java.util.ArrayList and java.util.List.

docs.title: Connect them
docs.text: Sixty minutes. Two relationships, both one-to-many, both with a rule.

docs.title: Students register for courses
docs.text:
• register(Course course) adds a course. A student may not hold more than six.
  • hasCourse(String courseCode) answers whether they are registered.
  • drop(String courseCode) removes one.
  • totalCredits() returns the sum of the credits of every course they hold.

Two decisions to make and defend.

What does register do when the student already has six? You met this in the lecture: return a value for outcomes the caller should expect, throw for situations the caller should have prevented. A student reaching their limit is a normal thing that happens. Decide, and be able to say why.

What does drop return when the course is not there? Same question, different shape.

totalCredits() is the important method here, and not because it is hard. Look at what it does: it walks the list and asks each course for its credits. It does not know how a course stores them, and it does not do anything to the course. That is delegation, and it is the point of the session.

docs.title: Professors teach courses
docs.text:
Same shape, different limit. A professor may not be assigned more than four courses.

  • assign(Course course)
  • totalTeachingCredits()

You will notice that Student.register and Professor.assign are nearly the same method with a different number in them. That is real duplication and it is genuinely annoying. You cannot fix it properly with what you know today. Write it twice, notice it, and bring the annoyance to week seven, where it is the whole topic.

docs.title: Never hand the list out
docs.text:
Both classes need a way to let the outside see the courses.

The version everybody writes first gives the caller your actual list, and then they can call clear() on it. Every rule register was enforcing is gone, and the class did it to itself in one line.

    public List<Course> getCourses() {
        return List.copyOf(courses);
    }

Be precise about what that protects. The list is a new one, so nobody can add to or clear yours. The courses in it are the same courses, because a list holds references. Somebody with the copy can still change a course's title. You have protected which courses the student holds, which is what was yours to protect.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
In UniversityApp:

Student ada = new Student("Ada Lovelace", 3.9, 2024);
Course java = new Course("CS101", "Programming in Java", 6, "Fall 2026");
Course maths = new Course("MA101", "Discrete Mathematics", 5, "Fall 2026");

ada.register(java);
ada.register(maths);

System.out.println(ada.getCourseCount());    // 2
System.out.println(ada.totalCredits());      // 11

for (Course course : ada.getCourses()) {
    System.out.println("  " + course.fullName());
}

Then register seven courses and watch the seventh be refused.

docs.title: Break them
docs.text:
Twenty minutes. Extend BreakIt from last week.

ada.getCourses().clear();
System.out.println(ada.getCourseCount());

The count must still be right and the clear() must fail. Read the exception and note which class threw it.

Then:

Course stolen = ada.getCourses().get(0);
stolen.setTitle("Nonsense");
System.out.println(ada.getCourses().get(0).fullName());

This one does change what the student sees, and it should. Write one sentence explaining why clear() was blocked and setTitle() was not. If you can answer that, you have understood both this session and week 2.

Then try these:

  • Register the same course twice. Does your code allow it? Should it?
  • Register a null course.
  • Drop a course that was never registered.
  • Assign a professor five courses.

Fix what you find. BreakIt scores zero again before you commit.

docs.title: Commit, and read the sprint
docs.text:
Fifteen minutes.

git add .
git commit -m "Week 4: students register for courses, professors teach them"
git push

Sprint 1 opens this week. Everything you need is in this module. You will build your own application, from your own classes, in this repository. The sprint brief is on the projects page.

The four commits in your history are worth looking at before you start. Week 1 is a design on paper. Week 2 is three classes that accept anything. Week 3 is the same classes refusing to be broken. Week 4 is a system. That progression is the thing you show somebody later, and it is why the commits matter more than the final state.

docs.title: Before you leave
docs.text:
• Student and Professor each hold a private final List
  • register and assign enforce their limits
  • totalCredits() asks each course rather than reaching into it
  • Neither class returns its internal list
  • BreakIt covers the new methods and scores zero
  • Pushed, with four weeks of history visible on GitHub

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
Let a course hold its students. The specification says a course knows who is enrolled in it. Add List<Student> to Course and an enrol method.

Now the hard part: if a student registers for a course, and the course also holds its students, both sides have to agree. Write down what goes wrong if only one side is updated, and what happens if you make each side update the other. There is a trap in that second idea and finding it is the exercise. This is a Module 2 topic and you are not expected to solve it today.

Department. Give it a List<Professor>, a facultyCount() and a totalTeachingLoad() that asks each professor. Three levels of delegation, department to professor to course, and no level reaches past the next one.

The rule nobody owns. "A course cannot be scheduled into a room too small for the students enrolled in it." It involves a course, a classroom and a count of students. Decide who enforces it and what they need to know. You raised this in week 1. See whether your answer has changed.

Back to the module

docs.title: Thinking in things
docs.text:
50 minutesWeek 1, session 1No prerequisites

By the end of this page you can look at a problem and describe it as a set of things that know something and can be asked to do something, rather than as a list of steps. You can also say who should be responsible for each rule in a system.

There is no Java on this page. Not one line. This session is about a way of seeing a problem, and you cannot see it clearly while you are also worrying about semicolons. The code starts in session 2.

docs.title: A cash machine, told twice
docs.text:
Here is a withdrawal at a cash machine, described the way you have always described programs.

Read the card. Look up the account. Check that the balance is enough. Check the daily limit. Subtract the amount. Count out the notes. Write a line in the log.

Seven steps in order. You could write that today.

Now here is the same withdrawal, described differently.

There is a card, which knows whose account it belongs to. There is an account, which knows its balance and decides whether a withdrawal is allowed. There is a cash drawer, which knows how many notes it holds and hands them out. There is a log, which records what happened.

The machine asks the card whose account this is. It asks the account to allow a withdrawal of fifty euro. The account decides, and says yes or no. If yes, the machine asks the drawer for the notes and tells the log.

Same machine. Same money. Nothing has been added and nothing has been removed.

What changed is where you put the boundaries. The first description cuts the problem into steps. The second cuts it into things.

That is the whole paradigm. Everything else this semester is consequences.

One problem cut into steps, and the same problem cut into thingsThe upper half shows five steps in a row, each joined by a line to a single shared store of data underneath, and the lines cross one another. The lower half shows three boxes named Card, Account and Cash drawer, each listing what it knows and what it does, joined to each other by two connections.Cut into stepsread cardcheck limitsubtractdispensewrite logthe balance, the daily limit, the notes, the logEvery step needs the data, so the data belongs to nobody in particular.Cut into thingsCardAccountCash drawerknows: whoseknows: balanceknows: notes leftdoes: identifydoes: allow, refusedoes: hand outEach thing keeps what it knows and decides what it does.

Look at the top half again. Five steps, one pile of data, and every step reaching into it. Nothing in that picture is responsible for the balance. The balance is just lying there.

docs.title: A thing knows, and a thing does
docs.text:
An object is not complicated. It is two things bolted together, and it is worth saying the definition plainly because everything else rests on it.

An object holds what it knows and what it doesA single box named Account divided into two columns. The left column lists what it knows: the balance, who owns it, whether it is frozen. The right column lists what it does: accept a deposit, allow a withdrawal, refuse one.AccountIt knowsIt doesthe balancewho owns itif it is frozenaccept a depositallow a withdrawalrefuse oneWhat it knows is its state. What it does is its behaviour. One thing holds both.

The left column is called state. The right column is called behaviour. Those are the only two words you need this week.

Notice the third item on the right. An account can refuse. That is not decoration, it is the point. A thing that can only hand over its data is a container. A thing that can say no is an object.

docs.title: Who is responsible?
docs.text:
Here is the question that turns this from a nice picture into a design skill.

Take any rule in the system. "A withdrawal cannot exceed the balance." Then ask two things.

Who should know this? The rule is about a balance. One thing in the system owns a balance. So the account should know it.

Who should decide? Whoever knows. If the account knows the balance and knows the rule, the account decides. Nobody else needs to.

Work through the cash machine and it resolves quickly. The daily limit is about the card, so the card knows it. How many notes are left is about the drawer, so the drawer decides whether it can pay out. The machine itself knows almost nothing. It just asks the right thing each time.

That is why "where does this code go" stops being a matter of taste. The code goes where the data is, because that is the only place the decision can be made honestly.

Verbs are not things

The most common first design has a class called WithdrawalManager or TransactionHandler or BalanceProcessor. It feels right, because withdrawing is clearly important.

Ask what it knows. Usually the answer is nothing. It holds no data of its own, so it spends its whole life reaching into other objects and changing their numbers for them. That is a step wearing a noun's name, and you have rebuilt the top half of the diagram with extra files.

If a class ends in Manager, Handler, Processor or Helper, stop and ask what it knows. There are real exceptions and you will meet one in Module 2, but they are exceptions and they still own something.

docs.title: Ask, do not take
docs.text:
The second half of the paradigm, and the half most courses skip.

You do not reach into someone's wallet and remove fifty euro. You ask them to pay you, and they decide whether they can. If they cannot, they say so. The money never leaves without the owner's agreement, and the owner is the only one who has to know how much is in there.

Programs work the same way, or they should.

Reaching into another object compared with sending it a requestIn the upper half a box named Cashier sends an arrow that passes straight through the wall of a box named Account and changes the balance inside it, with no rule consulted. In the lower half the Cashier sends a request named withdraw to the boundary of the Account, and the Account decides and sends an answer back.TakingCashierAccountbalanceno rule was askedbalance = balance - 50The wall is open. The account never found out, and never agreed.AskingCashierAccountbalancechecks its own rulewithdraw 50yes, or no

In the top picture the cashier knows how an account stores its money, so if that ever changes, the cashier breaks. In the bottom picture the cashier knows only what to ask for. The account can change everything about how it works, and nobody outside notices.

The difference between those two pictures is the difference between a program you can change and one you cannot.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
This is not free, and you should hear that from me rather than discover it while resenting me.

You will write more files. You will spend time deciding what to call things, and some of those decisions will feel arbitrary. Following what happens during a single operation means reading three small files instead of one big function, which is genuinely harder the first few times.

For a fifty-line script that you will run once and delete, none of this is worth it. Write the steps. Go home.

It becomes worth it the moment somebody changes the requirements, which in this course is every week and at work is every day.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text:
\"So we are modelling the real world\"

Nearly, and the gap matters.

You are modelling the problem, not reality. A real bank has buildings, regulators, a marketing department and a coffee machine. None of those belong in your program. And in Module 3 you will build a Transaction and in Module 4 a Controller, neither of which is a thing you could point at in a bank.

Ask what needs to exist for this program to be correct and easy to change. That question keeps working. "What exists in the world" stops working around week six.

\"So object orientation is about inheritance\"

That is the part most courses lead with, which is why people finish them able to recite four words and unable to design anything.

Inheritance is one tool for sharing behaviour between classes, and Module 2 covers it properly, including when using it is a mistake. It is not what objects are for. If you finish this module able to design good classes and unable to spell extends, you are in a better position than the reverse.

\"This is the right way to write software\"

No. It is one way, and this course teaches it because it is the one you will meet most often and because it teaches you to think about design.

In week twelve you will write Java in a different style, where data does not change and you transform it instead of asking it to change itself. Some problems fit that far better. Knowing both, and knowing when each is awkward, is worth more than believing in either.

If you remember one thing. An object is a thing that knows something and can be asked to do something. Designing is deciding who knows what, and therefore who decides what.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
Cut a problem you were not shown

A university library lends books to students. A book can be borrowed if a copy is available. A student cannot borrow more than five books at once. Overdue books carry a fine.

On paper. No Java, so nobody can hide behind syntax.

  1. Name three or four things. Not ten.
  2. For each, write what it knows.
  3. For each, write what it does, including at least one thing it can refuse.
  4. Write one sentence describing how a book gets borrowed, using only "X asks Y to ...". No thing is allowed to reach into another and change its data.

Then the hard part. The rule "a student cannot borrow more than five books" needs an owner. Whoever you chose, write down what that thing must already know in order to decide. If it does not know it, your design has a gap. Finding that on paper costs nothing. Finding it in week nine costs a weekend.

Bring it to the seminar. There is more than one defensible answer and the argument is the lesson.

docs.title: Think about it
docs.text:
1. Both descriptions of the cash machine are accurate, and the first one is shorter. So what has the second one actually bought, given that the money moves either way? Now suppose the bank adds an overdraft, and then a second kind of account with different rules.

  2. The account can refuse a withdrawal. That means the cashier has to cope with being told no. Has the cashier's job got easier or harder? Answer honestly, then say who you would rather be if the rule changes next month.

  3. You were told to ask what a class knows, and to be suspicious of one that knows nothing. Try to think of something in a program that genuinely has no data of its own but still deserves to exist as a thing. Bring the best example you can find, even if you are not sure it is right.

  4. The cash machine description gave the log its own box. A log only records what other things did. Does it know anything? Does it decide anything? Argue either way, and notice which of your two answers you would defend in front of the room.

docs.title: The university system
docs.text:
ReferenceWeeks 1 to 4Used in every seminar

This is the problem you build in the seminars. It is deliberately not the bank from the lectures.

Following a worked example teaches you the syntax. Building something you have not been shown teaches you the skill, and the skill is what the exam and the sprints ask for. You will be stuck more often here than in the lectures. That is the point of the seminar.

docs.title: The scenario
docs.text:
A university runs courses. Each course has a code, a title and a number of credits, and it runs in a particular semester.

Students enrol at the university in a given year and have a grade point average that changes as they complete courses. A student can register for courses, but not for more than six at a time.

Professors are employed by the university, each with a specialisation and a number of years of experience. A professor teaches courses. Nobody may be assigned more than four courses in a semester.

Courses are taught in classrooms. A classroom has a capacity, and a course cannot be scheduled into a room too small for the students enrolled in it.

Departments group professors together. Each department has a head.

That is everything. Read it slowly, because in the week 1 seminar you design the system from this paragraph alone.

docs.title: Rules for all of them
docs.text:
One constructor. It takes everything the object needs to be usable. There is no empty constructor, because an object with no id and no name is not a student.

Fixed fields have a getter and no setter. An id does not change. In week 3 they also become final, so the compiler enforces it rather than your memory.

No class prints anything. No displayStudentInfo(), no System.out.println inside a method. toString() returns text and main decides what to show. Week 13 puts a window on this and nothing in these classes will change.

Behaviour, not just storage. academicStanding() and academicTitle() are the interesting part. A class that is only fields with getters and setters has not been designed, it has been typed.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
• Class names singular and capitalised: Student, not Students.
  • Fields and methods in camelCase.
  • Ids are String, so "S-1001" rather than 1001. Nobody does arithmetic on an id.
  • Methods that answer a question start with is or can: isExperienced, canAccommodate.
  • Methods that do something are verbs: updateGpa, completeAnotherYear.

Consistent names matter more than you expect. When you ask for help in week 9, "my updateGpa throws" is a question somebody can answer in ten seconds.

Week 1 seminar. Setting up and designing

docs.title: What belongs to whom
docs.text:
50 minutesWeek 3, session 2Needs: Objects that refuse

By the end of this page you can decide whether a value belongs to one object, to the class as a whole, or should never change at all, and you can write each of those in Java. Your accounts will also start giving themselves account numbers.

Two questions run through this session, and they are the same question asked twice. Where does this value live? And when is it allowed to change? Getting those right is most of what separates a class that survives contact with a real system from one that quietly rots.

docs.title: Some things are decided once
docs.text:
An account number is chosen when the account is opened and then never again. Change it and every record referring to that account is now pointing at nothing.

Right now nothing stops it. There is no setAccountNumber, which helps, but a year from now somebody adds one because they need it for an import script, and the damage happens in a place nobody is looking.

    private final String accountNumber;

final on a field means it is assigned exactly once, in the constructor, and after that the compiler refuses. Not a convention, not a comment. Try to reassign it anywhere and the code does not build.

Use it for identity. An account number, a customer ID, a date of birth. Anything whose whole purpose is to stay the same is a candidate, and making it final costs one word and removes a category of bug permanently.

ownerName stays non-final, because people really do change their names and the bank really does have to record it.

docs.title: Objects that never change at all
docs.text:
Take that idea further. If every field of a class is final and no method changes anything, then the object cannot change after it is created. That is an immutable object.

You already use one constantly.

String name = "ada lovelace";
name.toUpperCase();
System.out.println(name);      // ada lovelace, unchanged

Everybody gets caught by this once. toUpperCase did not change the string, because a String cannot be changed. It made a new one and handed it back, and you threw it away.

name = name.toUpperCase();     // keep the new one

That is not a quirk. It is why you can hand a String to any method in the world without worrying about what it does to your copy. Nothing can do anything to it.

The same reasoning applies to anything that records a fact rather than tracking a state. A transaction record should be impossible to edit after it is written, which is exactly what an audit trail means. You will build one in Module 3.

What a fully immutable class looks like 
public final class Branch {

    private final String code;
    private final String city;

    public Branch(String code, String city) {
        this.code = code;
        this.city = city;
    }

    public String getCode() {
        return code;
    }

    public String getCity() {
        return city;
    }
}

Every field final, no setters, nothing that changes anything. Hand this to any code you like. Nobody can alter it, so nobody has to check.

The class itself is final too, which stops anyone extending it and adding mutable state through the back door. That word means something you meet in week 7; for now it is a detail worth seeing rather than understanding.

docs.title: Some things belong to the class
docs.text:
Now the other question. Every account has its own balance, its own number, its own owner. Three accounts, three balances.

But the bank needs unique account numbers, and the counter that produces them belongs to no single account. It belongs to all of them, which is to say it belongs to the class.

public class Account {

    private static int lastNumberIssued = 1000;

    private final String accountNumber;
    private String ownerName;
    private double balance;

    public Account(String ownerName, double openingBalance) {
        lastNumberIssued++;
        this.accountNumber = "AC-" + lastNumberIssued;

        this.ownerName = requireText(ownerName, "Owner name");

        if (openingBalance < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                    "Opening balance cannot be negative: " + openingBalance);
        }
        this.balance = openingBalance;
    }

static means there is exactly one lastNumberIssued, no matter how many accounts exist. Not one per account. One, full stop.

The constructor no longer takes an account number, because the account now issues its own. That is a real improvement: nobody outside can pick a number, so nobody outside can pick one that is already taken.

Instance fields compared with a static fieldThree Account objects each hold their own balance and account number. A separate box outside all of them holds a single static counter named lastNumberIssued, and each object has a line to that one shared box rather than holding its own copy.One per objectAccountAccountAccountAC-1001AC-1002AC-1003500.002500.001500.00One for the whole classstaticlastNumberIssued1003Three balances. One counter. Every account reads and updates the same one.

A static method belongs to the class too, and can be called without any object.

    public static int getAccountsOpened() {
        return lastNumberIssued - 1000;
    }

Account ada  = new Account("Ada Lovelace", 500.00);
Account alan = new Account("Alan Turing", 2500.00);

System.out.println(Account.getAccountsOpened());   // 2

Called on the class, not on an object, because the answer is not about any particular account.

A static method cannot touch instance fields or use this, and once you see why, it stops feeling like a rule. There is no object involved, so there is no balance to read. Which account's balance would it be?

Remember requireText from last session. It reads no fields and writes no fields; it just checks a string. It should be static.

    private static String requireText(String value, String label) {
        if (value == null || value.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(label + " is required");
        }
        return value;
    }

This also explains something that has been annoying you since first year. main is static, so it runs before any object exists, which is why you cannot call an ordinary method from it without making an object first.

The static counter will bite you in week 11

lastNumberIssued lives in memory. Close the program and it is gone. Start it again and it goes back to 1000.

So in week 11, when you save your accounts to a file and load them back, the next account you open will be given a number that already belongs to somebody. Two accounts, one number, and every lookup after that returns whichever one it happened to find first.

This is not a mistake in the code above. It is the right way to learn static and it is genuinely how many small programs work. But real systems get their identifiers from something that survives a restart, usually a database. Remember this paragraph when week 11 arrives.

Static is not a way to avoid creating objects

The first thing most people do with static is discover it makes the compiler stop complaining in main, and then mark everything static until the errors go away.

What you get is a program with one copy of everything and no objects at all. That is the pile of shared data from week 1, rebuilt on purpose, with a class name in front of it.

Before writing static, finish this sentence: this value belongs to the class because ____. If you cannot, it belongs to an object.

If you remember one thing. For every value, ask where it lives and when it may change. One per object, one for the whole class, or never again after the moment it was set.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
Prove what is shared and what is not

Create three accounts without giving them numbers.

Account ada   = new Account("Ada Lovelace", 500.00);
Account alan  = new Account("Alan Turing", 2500.00);
Account grace = new Account("Grace Hopper", 1500.00);

System.out.println(ada);
System.out.println(alan);
System.out.println(grace);
System.out.println(Account.getAccountsOpened());

You should get three different account numbers and a count of 3. If all three accounts have the same number, lastNumberIssued is not being incremented before it is used.

Now deposit into alan only and print all three. One balance moves. The counter is shared, the balances are not, and seeing both facts in the same run is the point.

Finally, add this line and read the compiler error:

ada.accountNumber = "AC-9999";

You will get two complaints, not one, and they are for different reasons. Work out what both of them are. That pair of errors is this whole session in one screen.

docs.title: Think about it
docs.text:
1. The account number is final, so it can never change. But a bank might genuinely need to renumber accounts after a merger with another bank. Does final make that impossible, or just make it obvious? Describe what you would actually have to do.

  2. lastNumberIssued is shared by every account ever created, which is convenient and also means every account is coupled to every other one. Name something that could go wrong because of that sharing, other than the restart problem already described.

  3. A String cannot be changed, so every operation on it makes a new one. That sounds wasteful. Why would the designers of Java accept that cost? Think about who receives strings and what they would otherwise have to check.

  4. You now have three places a value can live: in an object, in the class, or nowhere because it is computed when asked. A customer's total holdings could be any of those three. Argue for one, then find the situation that breaks your choice.

Week 4, session 1. Many objects

docs.title: Why objects
docs.text:
50 minutesWeek 1, session 2Follows: Thinking in thingsLecture code

By the end of this page you can explain why a rule that lives away from its data is optional, say precisely what Java adds to the C you already know, and pick out which things in a problem should be classes and which should not.

Last session made a promise: things that own their data survive change better than steps that share it. That is easy to say and easy to nod along to. This session tests it on code you have actually written.

docs.title: A program you already wrote
docs.text:
Something like this, in C, in your first year. Names and grades for a class.

char  names[100][50];
float grades[100];
int   count = 0;

void add_student(const char *name, float grade) {
    strcpy(names[count], name);
    grades[count] = grade;
    count++;
}

float average(void) {
    float total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        total += grades[i];
    }
    return total / count;
}

Sixty lines, it works, you got the mark. There is nothing wrong with it.

docs.title: Four changes later
docs.text:
Change one. Grades must be between 0 and 10. You add a check to add_student.

Change two. Grades can now be imported from a file. The import function writes into grades too, so the check goes there as well. Two copies.

Change three. A teacher can correct a grade after entry. Another function, another copy. Three.

Change four. Someone, possibly you at 2am, writes this in the middle of an unrelated function:

grades[3] = 11.0;

That compiles. It runs. No check was consulted, because checks live in functions and this line did not call one.

Now answer a simple question: where is the rule about grades in this program?

You cannot point at it. It is not in the program. It is in your head, and in the head of everyone else who has ever touched this file, and it survives exactly as long as all of you keep remembering it.

\"But I would never write grades[3] = 11.0\"

Maybe not today. You will write it in week eleven when you are tired and the deadline is tomorrow, and it will work, and you will move on.

The point is not that you are careless. It is that the program offers no resistance. A design that depends on everyone being careful forever is not a design. It is a hope.

docs.title: And then it gets worse
docs.text:
Now drop a student who left the course. You shift names down by one. You shift grades down by one.

Anything holding index 3 is now pointing at a different student. And next month, when somebody adds emails[100] and forgets to shift it too, nothing breaks. No crash, no compiler error. The program keeps running and quietly reports the wrong email for every student after position three.

That is the failure that costs a weekend, because it never announces itself.

docs.title: Why this happened
docs.text:
Look at how the program was split. add_student, average, print_all, load_file. Split by what it does, exactly like the top half of last session's diagram.

Every one of those needs the data, so the data has to be reachable from all of them, which means file scope, which means reachable from everything else in the file too.

Reachable by everything means changeable by everything. And when every function shares responsibility for keeping the data correct, nobody has it.

This is not a C problem. You can write the same design in Java, Python or JavaScript, and people do, every day. The language does not save you. The way you divided the work does.

docs.title: You already half solved this in C
docs.text:
Here is the part worth noticing. You do not need a new language to fix the drift.

struct Student {
    char  name[50];
    float grade;
};

struct Student students[100];

A student is now one thing. Delete students[3] and the name and grade go together, because they were never apart. You cannot shift one without the other.

So grouping data is not what Java is for. C does that, and you already knew how.

What C will not do is this:

students[3].grade = 11.0;   /* still compiles, still runs */

The struct holds the data together. It does not defend it. There is still no way to make the account refuse.

docs.title: What Java adds
docs.text:
Two things, and one you will not need until week seven.

The behaviour is attached to the thing. withdraw is not a function that happens to take an account. It is something an account does. That is "ask, do not take" from last session, turned into something you can actually write down: the request has somewhere to arrive.

The compiler decides who may touch the data. Mark a field private and students[3].grade = 11.0 stops being a line you should not write and becomes a line that does not compile. The rule stops being a convention and becomes something the machine checks, on every build, for everyone on the team, forever.

The third one is that a single request can run different code depending on what the thing actually is. That sounds strange now. Week seven.

If you remember one thing. C already lets you group data. What Java adds is a compiler that enforces who is allowed to change it.

docs.title: The rule, moved inside
docs.text: The same rule scattered across functions, and the same rule inside an objectThe upper half shows an array of balances with three separate functions below it, each connected to the array and each containing its own copy of the balance check. The lower half shows a single Account box containing both the balance and the withdraw method, with the check written once inside it.Data here, rules over therebalances{ 500.00, 1200.00, 30.00 }anyone can reach itwithdraw()transfer()monthlyFee()checks the balancechecks it againand againOne rule, written three times. Nothing stops a fourth place forgetting it.Data and its rules togetherAccountbalanceonly this object touches itwithdraw()the rule, written onceThe rule cannot be skipped, because it is part of the thing it protects.

docs.title: The first class
docs.text:
This is the account from last session, written down. We will build it together in the lecture, so watch rather than type.

public class Account {

    private double balance;

    public Account(double openingBalance) {
        this.balance = openingBalance;
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }

    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0 || amount > balance) {
            return false;
        }
        balance -= amount;
        return true;
    }
}

You are not expected to write this yet. Week 2 teaches every line. Five things to notice, and no more.

balance is private. That is the compiler enforcing the wall from last session's diagram.

The rule is inside, once. One place subtracts from a balance, so one place changes when the overdraft policy arrives.

withdraw can say no. The account decides, exactly as it did when the description was in English.

There is no index. An account is one thing, so its balance cannot drift away from its owner.

And withdraw does not print anything. It reports what happened and lets the caller decide what to say about it. That is deliberate, and in week ten you will be glad of it.

Account ada = new Account(500.00);

ada.withdraw(200.00);   // true, balance is now 300.00
ada.withdraw(900.00);   // false, balance is unchanged

docs.title: Which things become classes
docs.text:
Last session you cut a problem into things on paper. Now the same skill with a filter, because not every thing you named deserves a class.

Three questions.

Does it have data of its own that must stay correct? An account has a balance. It has to be right, and it changes over time.

Are there rules about that data? You cannot withdraw more than the balance. Somebody must enforce that, and the best somebody is whoever owns the data.

Can you ask it to do something? You ask an account to accept a deposit. You do not ask a monthly total to do anything. You just calculate it.

Run those over a bank:

Thing Class? Why Account Yes Owns a balance, has rules, can be asked things Customer Yes Owns a name and a set of accounts Transaction Yes A record of what happened, with details of its own Balance No A number that belongs to an account Interest rate No A value, until the rules around it get complicated Total holdings No Calculated from accounts, not a thing that exists Withdrawing No Something an account does, not a thing

The bottom three are where people go wrong, and they are the Manager trap from last session in a different costume.

docs.title: Common misreadings
docs.text:
\"Then everything should be private with a getter and a setter\"

A class where every field is private and every field has a public getter and a public setter is not protected. It is the same open data with four extra lines per field, and setBalance hands back exactly the power that private took away.

Ask what the thing is for. Account exposes withdraw, not setBalance, because withdrawing is what a bank account does and setting the balance to an arbitrary number is not. Week 3 is about this distinction.

\"My program works, so the design is fine\"

Working is the minimum, not the goal. The grade tracker at the top of this page works too.

Design is about what happens when the requirements change, and in this course they change every week on purpose. Sprint 2 is you rewriting Sprint 1 after you have felt the cost of your first design.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
Do this on your own code, not on mine

Find a program you wrote last year in C. Any of them, as long as it was more than about fifty lines.

  1. Pick one change that was asked of you after you first wrote it, or invent a plausible one now.
  2. Count the places in the file you had to edit, or would have to edit.
  3. For each edit, write down what you had to already know in order to get it right. Not what you typed. What you had to know.
  4. Find one piece of data in that program that any function could change, and name one rule about it that exists only in your head.

That last one is the point of the session. Everyone will find one. Bring it to the seminar, because comparing them is more convincing than anything on this page.

docs.title: Think about it
docs.text:
1. The grade rule lived in three functions and in your head. If you had written it in a comment at the top of the file, would anything have improved? Say precisely what a comment does and does not do. Now suppose the person reading that file next year does not speak your language.

  2. A struct fixed the parallel arrays, and it is available in C. So why did anyone bother inventing classes, when the drift problem was already solved? Answer without using the word encapsulation.

  3. private stops outside code from changing the balance. But withdraw is public, so outside code can still reduce it. What exactly was gained, if the money still leaves? Now a new rule arrives: withdrawals over 10,000 euro need a manager's approval. Where does it go, and how much existing code has to change?

  4. withdraw returns true or false and says nothing about why it failed. Was the amount negative, or was there not enough money? Decide whether that difference matters to whoever called it, and if it does, say what you would rather it returned. There is no clean answer available to you yet, which is why the question is here.

Weeks 5 to 8Module 2 of 48 lectures, 4 seminarsSprint 2 opens in week 8

One class is easy. This module is about what happens when there are several of them, several kinds of them, and they have to work together. By the end you can decide which class owns a piece of work, say what makes two of your objects the same object, and choose between inheritance and holding another object rather than guessing.

Module 1 taught you to build one good object. If you can do that, this module is the one that turns it into a design.

docs.title: Enumerations
docs.text:
A fixed set of values the compiler checks

50 minutesWeek 6, session 2Needs: The Single Responsibility PrincipleLecture code

What you will learn

  • How to replace a set of strings with a type whose values the compiler checks
  • How each value of that type can carry data of its own
  • How to tell what an enum can solve from what it cannot

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Grace's café takes orders on a printed slip. Next to Size, the slip has an empty line, and customers write whatever they like on it.

Over one morning, customers write "large", "Large", "L", "big" and "venti". The barista has to guess what each one means. "Big" is probably large. "Venti" is a size from another café entirely. One customer writes "medum".

Nobody did anything strange. A blank line accepts anything, so anything is what Grace gets. The mistakes only come to light later, at the coffee machine, when someone has to decide what was meant.

Now picture the same slip with three boxes to tick: ☐ Small ☐ Medium ☐ Large. Every slip is now readable. There is no way to write "medum", because there is nothing to write.

Programs have blank lines too. How do you give a Java program boxes to tick?

docs.title: A fixed list of options
docs.text:
The tick boxes work because the list of options is decided once, when the slip is printed, and nothing outside that list can appear. A slip can be wrong in only one way: a customer can tick the wrong box. It can no longer be unreadable.

A free-text field compared with tick boxesTwo order slips. On the left, a slip with a blank size line, surrounded by the different things customers wrote: large, Large, L, big, venti and medum, several shown in a warning colour. On the right, a slip with three tick boxes, Small, Medium and Large, with Large ticked. Only the three listed options can appear.A blank lineBoxes to tickOrder slipSize:largeLargeLbigventimedumanything can be writtenOrder slipSmallMediumLargeonly these three can appearA blank line accepts anything. A list of boxes accepts only what is on the list.

docs.title: Options can carry information
docs.text:
Grace's menu says more than the names of the sizes. Each size comes with its own facts:

Size Volume Price Small 250 ml 1.50 EUR Medium 350 ml 2.00 EUR Large 450 ml 2.50 EUR

Once the order says "Large", the volume and the price follow from it. Nobody needs a separate price list kept somewhere else, because the facts travel with the option. Add a fourth size, and you add one row, with its facts, in one place.

docs.title: Where that stops working
docs.text:
The café also has a fixed list of payment methods: cash, card and voucher. It looks like the same kind of list, but look at what changes from one option to the next.

Options that differ in data compared with options that differ in behaviourTwo panels. On the left, coffee sizes Small, Medium and Large each carry a volume and a price, which are values and fit in a table. On the right, payment methods Cash, Card and Voucher each need a different procedure: count the change, ask the bank, check the expiry date. These are actions, not values.Differ in dataDiffer in behaviourSmallMediumLarge250 ml 1.50350 ml 2.00450 ml 2.50CashCardVouchercount the changeask the bankcheck the expiry datevalues: fit in a tablesteps: do not fit in a tableA fixed list works for both. Only the left side is fully described by its data.

The sizes differ in data: numbers you can write in a table. The payment methods differ in behaviour: each one needs a different procedure. "Count the change" is not a number you can put in a column. A fixed list still helps with payments, because it stops anyone writing "chequ" on the slip, but the list alone cannot say what each option does.

Keep that distinction in mind. It decides how far the tool in this lecture can take you.

docs.title: Naming it
docs.text:
Definitions

Enumeration (enum). A type with a fixed set of values, listed once in its declaration. Java's enum keyword creates one, and no value outside the list can exist.

Enum constant. One of those values, such as SAVINGS. Each constant is an object, created once when the program starts, so it can hold fields and answer method calls.

Type safety. The compiler's guarantee that a variable can only hold values of its declared type. With an enum, a misspelt constant is a compile error instead of a bug you find later.

docs.title: Account types were a blank line
docs.text:
In week 4 the bank kept its account types like this:

List<String> types = List.of("CHECKING", "SAVINGS", "DEPOSIT");

A String is the blank line on the slip. All three of these compile, and none of them works:

if (type.equals("checking")) { ... }   // never matches: wrong case
if (type.equals("CHEKING"))  { ... }   // never matches: typo
account.setType("CRYPTO");             // not an account type at all

The first two fail silently: the code runs, and a branch that should fire never does. The third succeeds, and now the bank holds an account of a type that does not exist. The compiler could have caught all three, but to the compiler any text is a perfectly good String.

docs.title: Tick boxes for account types
docs.text:
In its simplest form, an enum is just the list of options:

public enum AccountType {

    CHECKING,
    SAVINGS,
    TERM_DEPOSIT
}

Three values, and no way to create a fourth from outside. A field declared as AccountType can hold one of those three, or null, and nothing else. AccountType.CHEKING does not compile, so the typo is caught in the editor, before the program ever runs.

docs.title: Facts that travel with the type
docs.text:
Like the coffee sizes, each account type comes with facts of its own: a name a customer should see, and a monthly interest rate. Because each constant is an object, those facts can live on it:

public enum AccountType {

    CHECKING("Current account", 0.0000),
    SAVINGS("Savings account", 0.0025),
    TERM_DEPOSIT("Term deposit", 0.0040);

    private final String label;
    private final double monthlyInterestRate;

    AccountType(String label, double monthlyInterestRate) {
        this.label = label;
        this.monthlyInterestRate = monthlyInterestRate;
    }

    public String getLabel() {
        return label;
    }

    public double getMonthlyInterestRate() {
        return monthlyInterestRate;
    }

Each of the first three lines calls the constructor below it. SAVINGS is an object built once, with the label "Savings account" and the rate 0.0025, and it is the same object every time you write AccountType.SAVINGS.

The constructor cannot be public or protected. Only those three lines are allowed to call it, which is what keeps the list fixed.

An account type field pointing at one of three constant objectsOn the left, an Account object holds a number and a field called type. That field holds an arrow pointing at one of three objects on the right, which are the three constants of the AccountType enum. Each constant is an object holding its own label and its own monthly interest rate.AccountTypeAccountAC-1001typeCHECKINGSAVINGSTERM_DEPOSITCurrent account 0.0000Term deposit 0.0040Savings account 0.0025Three objects, built once. The field holds an arrow to one of them.

Account now has a field of this type, set once in the constructor:

    private final AccountType type;

docs.title: Data: interest without a single decision
docs.text:
Because the rate travels with the type, paying interest needs no decision about what kind of account this is:

    public double applyMonthlyInterest() {
        double interest = balance * type.getMonthlyInterestRate();
        balance += interest;
        return interest;
    }

This is the coffee price following from the size. Add a fourth account type with its own rate, and this method does not change at all. TypesApp runs it for one account of each type:

TERM_DEPOSIT   Term deposit      0.40% a month
