docs.title: values() and valueOf()
docs.text:
Every enum comes with two methods you do not write yourself. values() returns all the constants in the order they were declared, and the console builds its menu from it:

    private AccountType askForType() {
        AccountType[] types = AccountType.values();
        for (int i = 0; i < types.length; i++) {
            System.out.println("  " + (i + 1) + "  " + types[i].getLabel());
        }

  1  Current account
  2  Savings account
  3  Term deposit

The menu cannot fall out of step with the enum, because it is made from it. A fourth constant appears in the menu without a change to BankConsole.

valueOf() goes the other way, from text to a constant, and refuses text it does not recognise:

valueOf("SAVINGS")  : Savings account
valueOf("CRYPTO")   : No enum constant AccountType.CRYPTO

This is the one place where unchecked text can still try to get in, and it is exactly where you want the check: at the edge of the program, where text from outside becomes a value inside.

docs.title: Behaviour: withdrawing is a different story
docs.text:
Withdrawing is where the payment-methods problem comes back. How much may be taken out depends on the type, and it is not a number:

  • a current account may go down to zero;
  • a savings account must keep 100 EUR in;
  • a term deposit refuses every withdrawal.

Those are three different rules, like cash, card and voucher. No field on the enum can hold them, so Account.withdraw has to decide by type:

        boolean allowed = switch (type) {
            case CHECKING -> balance - amount >= 0.00;
            case SAVINGS -> balance - amount >= 100.00;
            case TERM_DEPOSIT -> false;
        };

This is a switch expression: it produces a value, here a boolean, and the arrow form runs exactly one branch. Because it produces a value, the compiler insists that every constant of AccountType is covered. Add a fourth constant and this line stops compiling:

error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values

That is the enum's type safety working for you again: the compiler finds the place you forgot.

--- Withdrawing: the rule is behaviour ---
500 from the current account : true
2000 from the savings account: false
100 from the savings account : true
100 from the term deposit    : false
The older switch statement

You will also see the older form, a switch statement that assigns inside each branch:

double lowestAllowed;
switch (type) {
    case CHECKING -> lowestAllowed = 0.00;
    case SAVINGS -> lowestAllowed = 100.00;
    case TERM_DEPOSIT -> { return false; }
    default -> { return false; }
}

A statement does not have to cover every constant, so the compiler cannot be sure lowestAllowed was given a value, and it makes you write a default branch. That branch hides a later mistake: add a fourth type, forget to update this switch, and the new type silently takes the default. Prefer the switch expression whenever you are choosing a value.

The switch expression is safe, but notice where the rules are. Everything that makes a savings account a savings account, its minimum balance and its withdrawal rule, sits inside Account, next to the rules for every other type. If more methods start to depend on the type, each one needs its own switch, and the rules for one kind of account end up spread across many methods. Next week takes the other approach and gives each kind of account a class of its own.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Showing name() to a person

System.out.println("Account type: " + type.name());

Account type: TERM_DEPOSIT

name() returns the constant exactly as it is written in the source code, in capitals and with an underscore. It is for code. A person should see the label. Keeping the two apart also means you can rename a constant without changing what users read.

Using an enum for a list that changes

An enum is fixed when the program is compiled. The account types a bank offers change rarely, and only when the bank changes its products, so an enum fits. The bank's branches, or the list of its customers, change while the program is running, and an enum cannot grow at run time. Those belong in ordinary data, such as a List you can add to.

docs.title: The bigger picture
docs.text:
Java's own library uses enums for fixed sets everywhere: DayOfWeek has exactly seven values, Month has twelve. Whenever you see a set of values that will not change while the program runs, and a typo in one of them would be a bug, an enum is usually the right tool.

The distinction from this lecture is worth carrying forward. When the options differ only in data, an enum with fields describes them completely, as it does for interest rates. When they differ in behaviour, an enum can still list them, but the behaviour has to live somewhere, and a switch over the type is only a first answer.

Can each constant have its own method?

Yes. Java lets each enum constant override a method with its own body, and you will meet code that does it. It works well for small, self-contained behaviour. When the behaviour grows, with state of its own or rules that change often, separate classes usually describe it better. That is the subject of next week.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• An enum is a type with a fixed list of values, checked by the compiler. A misspelt value does not compile.
  • Each constant is an object, so it can carry data, like a label and a rate, that travels with it.
  • values() lists every constant; valueOf() turns text into a constant and refuses anything else.
  • An enum fully describes options that differ in data. Options that differ in behaviour still need code that decides, and a switch expression at least makes the compiler check that every option is handled.

Key terms: enumeration, enum constant, type safety, switch expression.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Quick checks. Enum or not?

  1. The days of the week.
  2. The bank's branches in Tirana, Durrës and Vlorë.
  3. The card networks a payment terminal accepts.
  4. The grades a course can give, from A to F.
Answers
  1. Enum. The set is fixed and will not change.
  2. Not an enum. Branches open and close while the system is in use; keep them as data.
  3. It depends. If the list changes only with a new version of the software, an enum fits. If the bank adds networks without releasing new code, it belongs in data.
  4. Enum, and a good one: each grade can carry its grade points as a field. You will build this in the seminar.

Coding exercise

Add a fourth constant to AccountType, above TERM_DEPOSIT, so that the semicolon stays on the last line:

YOUTH_SAVINGS("Youth savings", 0.0030),

Compile. Read the error and find which line it points at. Then write the rule for the new type: a youth savings account may go down to zero, but no single withdrawal may be larger than 200 EUR.

Run TypesApp and the console. List every file you changed, and every place that started working without a change.

Think about it.

  1. valueOf("CRYPTO") throws an exception instead of returning null. Is that the right choice when the text came from a person typing in the console? What about when it came from a file saved by an older version of the program?

    Hint

    Think about what each caller would do with a null, and how soon a mistake would be noticed.

  2. In the seminar, students have a level (undergraduate, masters, doctoral) and a set of grades. For each, decide whether it is a fixed list that differs only in data, or one that differs in behaviour. Which rule about graduation will need a switch?

    Hint

    A maximum number of courses is data. "Doctoral students also need a submitted thesis" is a rule that applies to one level only.

docs.title: The Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
One class, one reason to change

50 minutesWeek 6, session 1Needs: Object EqualityLecture code

What you will learn

  • How to recognise a class that is doing several jobs at once
  • A practical test for "one job": who would ask for this to change?
  • Why the code that talks to the user belongs in a class of its own

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Grace Hopper runs a small café, and she does everything herself. She takes the orders at the counter, makes the coffee, and takes the payment. With ten customers a day, it works well.

Then, in the same week, three people ask for changes.

The owner wants the menu reworded, with the sizes renamed and the prices shown differently. The health inspector introduces a new rule about how long milk can stay out of the fridge. The bank replaces the card terminal, and payments now work in a different way.

All three changes land on Grace. While she is rewriting the menu, she gets the milk rule wrong. While she is learning the new terminal, the coffee goes cold. Every change, whatever it was about, disturbs everything else she does.

Grace is not bad at any of her jobs. So what exactly has gone wrong?

docs.title: Building the idea
docs.text:
Look at who asked for the changes. Three different people, with three different concerns: the owner cares about how things are presented, the inspector about how coffee is made, the bank about how money is handled. None of them cares about the other two.

That gives you a useful way to count jobs. Instead of asking "what does this person do?", ask "who could ask for this to change?" Grace has three answers, so she has three jobs, and every change from any of those three people goes through her.

Now split the work. A waiter takes the orders, a barista makes the coffee, a cashier takes the payment.

One person with three reasons to change, compared with three roles with one reason eachTwo panels. On the left, three people who can ask for changes, the owner, the inspector and the bank, each have an arrow pointing at a single box for Grace, who takes orders, makes coffee and takes payment. On the right, the same three people each have one arrow, pointing at a separate role: the owner at the waiter, the inspector at the barista, and the bank at the cashier.One person, three jobsThree roles, one job eachOwnerInspectorBankOwnerInspectorBankmenu wordingmilk rulecard terminalmenu wordingmilk rulecard terminalGraceorderscoffeepaymentWaiterBaristaCashierorderscoffeepaymentCount who can ask for a change: three people for Grace, one for each new role.

Each role now has exactly one person who can ask it to change. When the inspector's milk rule changes, only the barista needs to know. The waiter's menu and the cashier's terminal are not touched, so they cannot be broken by accident.

The roles still work together, and they do it by asking, as the objects did last week. The waiter does not walk into the kitchen and make the coffee. The waiter passes on the order, and the barista hands back a cup.

docs.title: The kitchen never talks to the customers
docs.text:
One of these splits deserves a closer look. Some roles do the work: the barista knows the recipes and the cashier knows the prices. One role talks to the customers: the waiter asks what they want and tells them what happened. The barista never needs to know whether the order came from a customer at the counter, a phone call, or an app.

The counter talks to customers, the kitchen does the workOn the left, a customer box exchanges messages with a waiter box: the customer gives an order and receives a sentence back. A dashed vertical line separates this counter side from the kitchen side on the right, where a barista box receives the order from the waiter and returns a cup. Only the order and the cup cross the line.Talks to peopleDoes the workCustomerWaiterasks, reportsBaristaknows the recipes"a latte""enjoy"ordercupOnly the order and the cup cross the line. The barista never speaks to a customer.

The payoff comes when the café changes how it serves people. Add a delivery app, and the app replaces the waiter: it asks for the order and reports what happened. The barista does not change at all, because the barista never knew who was asking.

The same shape appears in almost every program. One part does the work and keeps the rules. Another part deals with the people using it: reading what they type, showing them results. Keeping the two apart means either one can change without breaking the other.

docs.title: Naming it
docs.text:
Definitions

The Single Responsibility Principle. A class should have one reason to change. Put differently: one person, or one kind of request, should be able to ask for a change to it. The principle was named by Robert C. Martin, and it is the "S" in a set of design principles you will hear called SOLID.

Separation of concerns. Keeping code that deals with different concerns, such as business rules, presentation and storage, in different places, so that a change to one does not disturb the others.

Model and user interface. The model is the part of a program that holds the data and enforces the rules. The user interface is the part that talks to people. In the café, the barista and the cashier are the model, and the waiter is the user interface.

docs.title: In our bank
docs.text:
Open the main method you wrote for Sprint 1 and count its jobs. Most Sprint 1 programs do all of these in one method: read what the user typed, work out what they meant, find the right objects, do the arithmetic, decide whether it was allowed, and print a sentence about the result.

That is Grace on a busy day. The wording of the messages, the rules about money, and the way input is read all live in one method, so a change to any of them means reading all of them. The method cannot be called from anywhere else, and it cannot be tested, because a test cannot read what was printed on the screen.

Our bank had the same problem. In week 6 it is split the way the café was.

docs.title: Who could ask for a change?
docs.text:
Class Its one reason to change Account, Customer, Bank The bank changes its rules about money BankConsole The wording, the language or the menu changes ConsoleApp The way the program is put together changes

Account, Customer and Bank are the model, the kitchen. BankConsole is the user interface, the waiter. ConsoleApp is the owner who opens the café in the morning: it creates everyone and introduces them to each other.

docs.title: ConsoleApp: put it together and start
docs.text:
public class ConsoleApp {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Bank bank = new Bank("Bank of Tirana");
        seed(bank);

        Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
        BankConsole console = new BankConsole(bank, input);
        console.run();
    }

That is the whole main. It builds the model, builds the class that talks to the user, and hands one to the other. (seed adds Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing and Grace Hopper as customers, so there is something to look at.)

docs.title: BankConsole: the waiter
docs.text:
public class BankConsole {

    private final Bank bank;
    private final Scanner input;

    public BankConsole(Bank bank, Scanner input) {
        this.bank = bank;
        this.input = input;
    }

    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Welcome to " + bank.getName() + ".");

        boolean running = true;
        while (running) {
            printMenu();
            String choice = input.nextLine().trim();
            switch (choice) {
                case "1" -> listCustomers();
                case "2" -> openAccount();
                case "3" -> transfer();
                case "4" -> payInterest();
                case "0" -> running = false;
                default -> System.out.println(
                        "There is no option " + choice + ".");
            }
            System.out.println();
        }
        System.out.println("Goodbye.");
    }

Two things are worth noticing. BankConsole is handed the bank and the scanner instead of creating them, so the same console could be pointed at a different bank, such as a test bank full of sample data. And the menu uses the arrow form of switch, which runs exactly one branch, with no break needed. The next session looks at switch more closely.

docs.title: The console asks, the bank decides
docs.text:
Here is the handler for a transfer:

    private void transfer() {
        System.out.print("From account number: ");
        String from = input.nextLine().trim();
        System.out.print("To account number: ");
        String to = input.nextLine().trim();
        double amount = askForAmount("Amount: ");

        if (amount <= 0) {
            System.out.println("A transfer has to be a positive amount.");
            return;
        }

        // The console asks, the bank decides, the console reports.
        if (bank.transfer(from, to, amount)) {
            System.out.printf("Sent %.2f EUR.%n", amount);
        } else {
            System.out.println("That transfer did not go through.");
        }
    }

Look for any arithmetic, or any check on a balance. There is none. The console collects three pieces of text, asks the bank, and turns true or false into a sentence. This is the waiter passing an order to the kitchen and reporting back.

> From account number: To account number: Amount: Sent 200.00 EUR.
> From account number: To account number: Amount: A transfer has to be a positive amount.

You may have noticed that the amount is checked twice: here, and again inside Bank.transfer, which throws on a zero or negative amount. They are two different rules that happen to look alike. A person typing -5 is an ordinary mistake, so the console catches it and explains. Code calling transfer with -5 is a bug, so the bank refuses it loudly. Each check belongs to the class that is responsible for that kind of mistake.

The model on one side of a line and the console on the otherOn the left, three stacked boxes named Bank, Customer and Account make up the model, and none of them prints anything. A dashed vertical line separates them from the right side, where a ConsoleApp box hands control to a BankConsole box holding the Scanner, the printing and the menu. Two arrows cross the line: the console asks, and the model answers. Below the console sits a faint dashed box labelled as a window in week thirteen, showing what replaces it.The modelWhat the person seesBankCustomerAccountno println, no Scanner, anywhereConsoleAppBankConsoleScannerprintlnthe menua window, week 13asksanswersMethod calls cross the line. Nothing else does.

docs.title: Checking it yourself
docs.text:
This is a claim you can check rather than take on trust. Search Account.java, Customer.java, Bank.java and AccountType.java for System.out. In Eclipse, that is Ctrl+H, File Search.

0 results

Four classes, a few hundred lines, and not one of them prints anything. Every sentence the user sees comes from BankConsole.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Returning a sentence instead of printing one

A common half-fix is to stop printing and return the sentence instead:

// In Account. It prints nothing, and it is still the wrong place.
public String describe() {
    return "Account " + accountNumber + " holds " + balance + " EUR";
}

Nothing is printed, so it looks solved. But Account now owns the wording, the order of the information and the language. Translate the program, or show the balance in a table, and you are editing Account again. If a method's result is a sentence meant for a person, it belongs with the other sentences, in the user interface.

toString is the exception. It is there to help you while you write and debug code, not to talk to the user.

Printing from the model \"just for now\"

A System.out.println inside Account.withdraw that explains a refusal is genuinely useful while you are testing. It also means Account has decided it is talking to a terminal. Once the program has a window, that message goes nowhere. If you need to see what the model is doing, use the debugger, or ask the model for the information and print it from the console.

docs.title: The bigger picture
docs.text:
The split you made this week pays off twice later in the course. In week 10 you write tests, and a test can only check what a method returns, so methods that return results can be tested and methods that print cannot. In week 13 the program gets a window, and BankConsole is the one class that gets replaced.

Web and mobile applications are built the same way, usually with more layers: the screens you see, the code that handles requests, the business rules, the storage. Each layer changes for its own reasons, and different teams often own different layers.

Can you split too far?

Yes. One responsibility does not mean one method per class, and it does not mean dozens of tiny classes with names like AmountChecker and NameTrimmer. A responsibility is a reason to change, not a single action. Account both deposits and withdraws, and that is fine, because the same person, the bank's rule-maker, would ask for changes to both.

A useful sign that you have gone too far: to make one ordinary change, you have to edit five small classes that always change together. Then they are really one responsibility, spread too thin.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A class has one responsibility when only one kind of request could make it change.
  • "Who would ask for this to change?" is a more reliable test than "what does this class do?".
  • Keep the model, which holds the data and the rules, separate from the user interface, which talks to people.
  • In the bank, Account, Customer and Bank never print. BankConsole does all the reading and printing, and ConsoleApp puts them together.

Key terms: Single Responsibility Principle, separation of concerns, model, user interface.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Quick checks.

  1. Who could ask for a change to each of these: Account, BankConsole, and a class MonthlyReport that calculates the month's totals and also emails them to the manager?
  2. BankConsole is handed its Bank instead of creating one. Name one thing that makes possible.
  3. The bank decides that transfers over 10,000 EUR need a second approval. Which class changes?
Answers
  1. Account: whoever sets the bank's rules about money. BankConsole: whoever decides what the user sees and how. MonthlyReport: two different people, whoever defines the totals and whoever manages how reports are sent, so it has two responsibilities.
  2. The same console can be run against a different bank, for example one filled with test data, without changing BankConsole.
  3. Bank. It is a rule about money, so it belongs in the model. The console may need a new message too, but the decision itself lives in the bank.

Coding exercise

Add this line inside Account.withdraw, just before it returns false for a refused withdrawal:

System.out.println("Refused: not enough money in " + accountNumber);

Run the program and try a withdrawal that is too large. The message is useful. Now answer three questions in writing:

  1. Who reads that message in week 13, when the program has a window and no terminal?
  2. A test wants to check that taking 900 from an account holding 500 is refused. What can the test look at?
  3. The bank needs the message in Albanian. How many classes now contain user-facing text?

Then remove the line from Account and make BankConsole print an equivalent message when withdraw returns false. The behaviour is the same, and all three answers change.

Think about it.

  1. The amount is checked in BankConsole.transfer and again in Bank.transfer. Make the case that this is duplication and one check should go. Then make the case that they are two different rules. Which argument is stronger?

    Hint

    Ask who each check protects against. One protects against a person typing something wrong, the other against a programmer calling the method wrongly.

  2. Before the seminar, open your UniversityApp.main. List every job it does, and for each one, say who could ask for it to change. Which of those jobs should move into a UniversityConsole?

    Hint

    Anything that reads input or prints a sentence belongs in the console. Anything about students, courses and enrolment rules belongs in the model.

public Student(String studentId, String name, int enrolmentYear)

Class Compare on Not on Student the id the name, the year, the courses Professor the id the name Course the code the title, the credits, the semester

Student ada = new Student("Ada Lovelace", 2024);
Student same = new Student(ada.getStudentId(), "Ada Lovelace", 2024);

docs.title: The class
docs.text:
public class University {

    private final String name;
    private final List<Student> students = new ArrayList<>();
    private final List<Course> courses = new ArrayList<>();

Then the methods you already know the shape of:

docs.title: Capacity
docs.text: Add a maximum to Course, set in the constructor, and isFull(). A course cannot hold more students than its room.

docs.title: The method the session is about
docs.text:
public boolean enrol(String studentId, String courseCode)

Both sides of the relationship get updated here, and nowhere else. Write the checks in an order where the system is still correct at the end of every line:

  1. Student or course not found. Nothing has changed.
  2. Already enrolled. Nothing has changed.
  3. Student is at their course limit. Nothing has changed.
  4. Course is full. Nothing has changed.
  5. Only now, add the course to the student and the student to the course.

Then withdraw(String studentId, String courseCode), which undoes both sides.

Leaving register and enrol both public

Student.register from week 4 still exists and still works, and it only updates one side.

If both are public, somebody will call the wrong one and the two lists will disagree. Decide what happens to register. Making it package-private so only University can call it is one answer. There are others. Say which you chose and why.

docs.title: The check that proves it
docs.text:
Count the enrolments from both directions. They have to match.

    public int enrolmentsFromStudents()   // sum of each student's course count
    public int enrolmentsFromCourses()    // sum of each course's student count

Those two numbers must be equal after every operation, including the ones that failed. Print both after each enrol and each withdraw. This is the university's version of the bank total that never moves.

List<Course> list = ada.getCourses();
System.out.println(list.contains(javaCourse));

docs.title: Object Equality: equals and hashCode
docs.text:
Same object, or same thing?

50 minutesWeek 5, session 2Needs: Object CollaborationLecture code

What you will learn

  • The difference between two objects being identical and two objects being equal
  • How to decide what "equal" should mean for a class you design
  • How to write equals and hashCode so that Java's collections agree with your decision

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Open the contacts on your phone and you will probably find someone saved twice. Maybe your friend Ana appears as "Ana" and again as "Ana Hoxha (work)". Your phone notices and offers to merge the duplicates.

To do that, the phone has to answer a question that sounds simple: when are two contacts the same person?

Try a few answers.

Same name? Then two different friends who are both called Ana get merged into one, and you lose a contact.

Same name and same number? Then "Ana" and "Ana Hoxha (work)" are never merged, because the names differ, even though it is obviously the same person.

Same phone number? That is much closer. Ana can change how she is saved, or even change her surname, and she is still the same person, because her number has not changed.

Nobody could have answered this for the phone in advance. Somebody who understood what a contact represents had to make a decision. Java has exactly the same problem with your objects, and it leaves the decision to you.

docs.title: Building the idea
docs.text:
The word "same" is hiding two different questions.

Is it the same object? Your phone might show Ana under "Favourites" and under "Recent calls". Those are two ways of reaching one contact card. Edit the card in one place and the change appears in the other, because there is only one card.

Does it count as the same thing? The two cards "Ana" and "Ana Hoxha (work)" are separate cards. Editing one does not touch the other. Yet they describe the same person, and you would like the phone to treat them that way.

Same object compared with same thing, using phone contactsTwo panels. On the left, titled same object, two labels, Favourites and Recent calls, both point with arrows at a single contact card for Ana with her phone number. On the right, titled same thing, two separate contact cards, one saved as Ana and one saved as Ana Hoxha work, show the same phone number. A note between them asks whether they are the same person and says that you decide.Same objectSame thingFavouritesRecent callsAna069 000 1234AnaAna Hoxha (work)069 000 1234069 000 1234same person?you decideLeft: one card reached two ways. Right: two cards that may describe one person.

The first question has a fixed answer that never needs your help. The second question has no fixed answer, because it depends on what the thing represents. And once you look at a few examples, a pattern appears: things fall into two groups.

Some things are equal when everything about them matches. Two 10-euro notes are interchangeable when you pay for coffee. A date is a date: 5 November 2026 is the same day whoever writes it down. These are values.

Other things are equal when their identity matches, however much else changes. A person who changes their name is still the same person. A contact is the same contact as long as the number is the same. These have an identifier that says who they are, and everything else is just information about them.

Equal when Examples Value Every part matches An amount of money, a date, a colour, a point on a map Entity The identifier matches, whatever else has changed A person, a contact, an order, a bank account

docs.title: Finding duplicates quickly
docs.text:
There is one more part of the story. A phone with two thousand contacts cannot compare every card with every other card, because that is about two million comparisons. Instead it sorts the cards into groups, say by the first letter of the name, and only compares cards within the same group.

That works only if two cards that count as the same person always land in the same group. Look at what goes wrong here:

Two contacts for one person filed in different groupsFour drawers labelled A, B, an ellipsis, and H represent contacts grouped by the first letter of the name. A card saved as Ana with number 069 000 1234 sits in drawer A. A card saved as Hoxha, Ana with the same number sits in drawer H. The duplicate finder only compares cards inside each drawer, so these two cards, which count as the same person because their numbers match, are never compared.AB...HAnaHoxha, Ana069 000 1234069 000 1234BesaBledisame person, never comparedGrouped by the first letter of the nameEqual by number, grouped by name: the duplicate finder never sees the pair.

The phone decided that sameness depends on the number, but it chose the group using the name. The two cards for Ana sit in different drawers and are never compared, so the duplicate is never found.

The fix is a rule worth remembering: whatever information decides "same" must also decide the group. If cards are equal by number, group them by something taken from the number, such as its last digit. Then equal cards always land in the same group.

docs.title: Naming it
docs.text:
Definitions

Identity. Two references point to the very same object in memory. In Java, == tests identity.

Equality. Two objects count as the same thing according to a rule the class defines. In Java, the equals method tests equality, and you write that method.

Value and entity. A value is equal to another when all its parts match. An entity is equal to another when its identifier matches.

Hash code. A number calculated from an object, used by some collections to decide which group (Java calls it a bucket) the object goes into. It is computed by the hashCode method.

The hash code contract. Objects that are equal must have equal hash codes. This is the "same information decides the group" rule from the contacts story.

docs.title: Two objects, one account
docs.text:
The bank meets this problem as soon as account data comes from outside the program. When accounts are saved and loaded back, or arrive from another system, they already have numbers. Account has a second constructor for that case, which accepts an existing number instead of issuing a new one:

    public Account(String accountNumber, double balance) {

That means the program can end up holding two objects for one account: the one Ada opened, and a copy that came from outside.

Account account = ada.openAccount(500.00);
String number = account.getAccountNumber();

Account restored = new Account(number, 500.00);

Account AC-1001: 500.00 EUR
Account AC-1001: 500.00 EUR
account == restored      : false

== reports false. It is testing identity, and these are two separate objects. But anyone working at the bank would say they are the same account, just as the two cards are the same Ana.

So which kind of thing is an account? It has an identifier, the account number, and its balance changes every day without making it a different account. An account is an entity, and two accounts are equal when their numbers match.

Two objects for one account: identity says different, equality says the sameOn the left, two variables named account and restored each hold an arrow to a separate Account object. Both objects hold the number AC-1001; one holds 500 and the other 1500. Two labels sit between the objects. The first says double equals compares the arrows and gives false. The second says equals compares the numbers and gives true. The balance is shown faded, because it is not part of the comparison.VariablesObjectsaccountrestoredAccountAccountAC-1001AC-1001500.001500.00== compares arrowsfalseequals compares numberstrueTwo objects, so not the same arrow. One number, so the same account.

docs.title: Writing equals
docs.text:
Every Java class inherits an equals method from the built-in Object class, and by default it does the same as ==. To give Account the rule we just decided on, you replace that method with your own version. Replacing an inherited method like this is called overriding.

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object other) {
        if (this == other) {
            return true;
        }
        if (!(other instanceof Account)) {
            return false;
        }
        Account that = (Account) other;
        return accountNumber.equals(that.accountNumber);
    }

Read it as four short steps:

  1. this == other: if it is literally the same object, there is nothing to compare.
  2. other instanceof Account: the parameter is an Object, so someone could pass a String, or null. Both fail this test, which also saves you a separate null check.
  3. The cast is safe now, because step 2 proved that other is an Account.
  4. The decision: compare the account numbers, and nothing else.

@Override asks the compiler to confirm that you really are replacing an inherited method. You will see in a moment why that matters.

account == restored      : false
account.equals(restored) : true

docs.title: What equals gives you
docs.text:
Java's collections call equals whenever they search for something. Before Account had its own equals, a list could only find the exact object you put in. Now it can find the account:

List<Account> accounts = ada.getAccounts();
System.out.println("contains(restored)       : "
        + accounts.contains(restored));
System.out.println("indexOf(restored)        : "
        + accounts.indexOf(restored));

contains(restored)       : true
indexOf(restored)        : 0

Without your equals, those lines print false and -1.

This also explains the line in last session's Bank.transfer that refuses a transfer from an account to itself, from.equals(to). The decision about what makes two accounts the same now lives in one place, inside Account, and every other class simply asks.

The balance plays no part, exactly as we decided. After a deposit into the copy, the two still count as one account:

Account AC-1001: 1500.00 EUR
still equal              : true

docs.title: Writing hashCode
docs.text:
ArrayList searches by checking each element in turn, so it only needs equals. But Java also has HashSet and HashMap, which find things fast by sorting objects into buckets, just like the phone sorting contacts into groups. They choose the bucket from the object's hash code.

The default hashCode is based on the object's identity, so two separate objects almost always get different hash codes, and land in different buckets. For our two equal accounts, that is the "Ana under A, Hoxha under H" problem again:

A hash set files an object in one drawer and searches in anotherA row of five drawers numbered zero to four represents a hash set. In the top half, labelled add, an account object with number AC-1001 is filed in drawer one. In the bottom half, labelled contains, an equal account object with the same number is looked up. Without a matching hashCode its hash leads to drawer three, which is empty, so the search reports false even though an equal object is in the set.add(account)contains(restored)AC-1001AC-100101234AC-1001hash leads to drawer 1a different hash leads to drawer 3: emptyEqual objects with different hash codes are filed in one drawer and searched for in another.

The cure is the same as for the phone. Build the hash code from the same information that equals uses:

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(accountNumber);
    }

Objects.hash combines the fields you give it into one number. Give it exactly the fields that equals compares, no more and no fewer, and equal objects will always land in the same bucket.

equal objects            : true
equal hash codes         : true

docs.title: Customer is an entity too
docs.text:
A customer has an id, and the name is only information about them. So Customer makes the same decision:

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object other) {
        if (this == other) {
            return true;
        }
        if (!(other instanceof Customer)) {
            return false;
        }
        Customer that = (Customer) other;
        return customerId.equals(that.customerId);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(customerId);
    }

And just like Ana in the contacts, a customer who changes her name stays the same customer:

ada.setName("Ada Byron");
Customer found = bank.findCustomer(ada.getCustomerId());
System.out.println("after a name change      : " + ada.equals(found));

after a name change      : true

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Writing equals(Account other)

This compiles:

public boolean equals(Account other) {
    return accountNumber.equals(other.accountNumber);
}

It does not replace the inherited equals(Object). It adds a second method with the same name but a different parameter type, which is called overloading. Your own code might call the new method and seem to work. Java's collections only know about equals(Object), so contains, indexOf and remove quietly go back to comparing identity.

With @Override on it, the compiler checks that the method really does replace an inherited one, and refuses this version. Always put @Override on equals.

Writing equals and forgetting hashCode

Everything appears to work, because lists only use equals. The problem stays hidden until the first HashSet or HashMap in the program, possibly weeks later, in code that looks perfectly correct. The method that is wrong is not the one that fails, which is what makes this bug so hard to find. Write the two methods together, from the same fields.

docs.title: The bigger picture
docs.text:
Every database uses this idea. A table of customers has a primary key, an id column, and two rows describe the same customer exactly when their keys match. That is the entity decision, made by the people who designed the table.

Values get easier later in the course. In week 12 you will meet records, a kind of Java class that writes equals and hashCode for you from all of its fields. That suits values perfectly. For entities like Account, where only the identifier should count, you will still write them yourself.

instanceof or getClass()?

You will also see equals written like this:

if (other == null || getClass() != other.getClass()) {
    return false;
}

The difference only matters once one class extends another, which happens in week 7. With instanceof, a savings account and a plain account with the same number count as equal. With getClass(), they do not. Which is right depends on what you mean. This course uses instanceof, because an account number identifies one account at one bank, whatever kind of account it is.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• == tests identity: are these the very same object?
  • equals tests equality: do these count as the same thing? You decide what that means.
  • Values are equal when all their parts match. Entities, such as accounts and customers, are equal when their identifiers match.
  • Equal objects must have equal hash codes, so build hashCode from exactly the fields equals uses.

Key terms: identity, equality, value, entity, overriding, overloading, hash code, hash code contract.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Quick checks.

  1. For each of these, would equals compare one identifying field or every field? An amount of money with a currency. A customer. A transaction with a transaction id. A date.
  2. After restored.deposit(1000.00), what does account.equals(restored) return?
  3. equals compares account numbers, but hashCode is built from the balance. Two equal accounts hold different balances. Is the contract broken?
Answers
  1. Money: every field, so the amount and the currency, because it is a value. Customer: the id. Transaction: its id. Date: every field, because it is a value.
  2. true. The balance is not part of the decision.
  3. Yes. The accounts are equal but will almost certainly have different hash codes, so a HashSet can store one and fail to find the other. The hash code must come only from fields that equals compares.

Coding exercise

First, add the balance to the comparison in Account.equals:

return accountNumber.equals(that.accountNumber)
        && balance == that.balance;

Run EqualityApp and look at "still equal" after the deposit. Write one sentence on what is wrong with an account that stops being itself when money is paid in. Then put it back.

Second, delete hashCode from Account entirely and run EqualityApp again. Everything looks fine. Now add these lines at the end of main, with import java.util.HashSet; and import java.util.Set; at the top:

Set<Account> set = new HashSet<>(List.of(account));
System.out.println("set.contains(restored)   : "
        + set.contains(restored));

Explain the result using the contacts story, then put hashCode back and run it once more.

Think about it.

  1. One Account object was loaded from last night's backup, and another is the live one. Their balances differ, and equals says they are the same account. Is that a problem with equals, or with something else? Who should decide which balance is right?

    Hint

    equals answers "is this the same account?", not "is this information up to date?". Those are different questions, and they may belong to different classes.

  2. The bank discovers that customers C-1001 and C-1340 are the same person, who registered twice. This is the contacts problem again. What does equals say about them now, what should it say, and what would it cost to make it say that?

    Hint

    equals can only be as good as the identifier it compares. Where would a better identifier come from, and what happens to the accounts already attached to each id?

docs.title: Object Collaboration: Responsibility and Delegation
docs.text:
When a rule needs more than one object

50 minutesWeek 5, session 1Needs: Objects that own other objectsLecture code

What you will learn

  • How to recognise a rule that involves more than one object
  • How to decide which class should be responsible for it
  • How objects delegate work to each other instead of reaching into each other's data

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Think about a football transfer. Ardi plays for Riverside FC, and Hillside FC wants to sign him.

Each club keeps its own squad list, and each club is careful with it. A club will not register the same player twice. A club will not release a player it does not have, and it can refuse to release one whose contract has not ended. Every one of those rules is about one club and its own list, and each club can enforce them by itself.

The transfer takes two steps. Riverside releases Ardi, and Hillside registers him.

Now suppose someone does it in the other order. Hillside registers Ardi first. Then Riverside is asked to release him and refuses, because his contract runs until the summer. Riverside was entitled to say no. Hillside did nothing wrong either; it registered a player, which is what registering is.

And yet Ardi is now on two squads at once, and could in principle play for both.

Which club made the mistake? Neither of them. The rule that broke, a player is registered with exactly one club, does not belong to Riverside or to Hillside. It is a rule about the two of them together. So who is supposed to enforce it?

docs.title: Building the idea
docs.text:
Every rule you have written so far in this course has belonged to one object. An account refuses a negative deposit. A customer refuses a blank name. Each object guards its own data, and because that data is private, nobody else can break its rules.

The transfer rule is a different kind of rule. To check it, you have to be able to see both clubs at the same time, and neither club can. Riverside has no idea what is on Hillside's list, and that is how it should be.

So ask the question directly: in this picture, who can see both clubs?

A rule between two clubs, first with no owner and then owned by the federationTwo panels. On the left, two club boxes named Riverside FC and Hillside FC each hold a short squad list and their own rules. Above them floats a dashed box reading: a player is registered with exactly one club, followed by a question mark, because neither club owns that rule. On the right, the same two clubs sit below a box labelled Federation, which owns the rule. An arrow labelled release goes from the federation down to Riverside, and an arrow labelled register goes down to Hillside.Nobody owns the ruleThe federation owns itRiverside FCHillside FCRiverside FCHillside FCArdiBesaDrenEraArdiBesaDrenEraown rulesown rulesown rulesown rulesa player is registeredwith exactly one club?Federationowns the rulereleaseregisterEach club guards its own list. A rule about both lists needs someone who sees both.

The federation can. It knows every club and every registration, and in real football this is exactly how it works: a new club cannot register a player until the federation confirms that the old registration has ended. The rule lives with the one party that can see the whole picture.

Notice how the federation goes about it. It does not reach into Riverside's squad list and cross Ardi out. It asks Riverside to release him, and Riverside applies its own rules, contract and all, before answering yes or no. Only then does the federation ask Hillside to register him. The clubs keep full control of their own lists. The federation adds one thing that neither club could provide: the decision about what happens, and in which order.

docs.title: Order matters
docs.text:
That order is worth a closer look, because it is what went wrong at the start.

Of the two steps, only one can fail. Riverside might refuse to release Ardi. Registering a free player at Hillside, on the other hand, always works. So do the step that can fail first. If Riverside refuses, nothing has happened yet, and there is nothing to undo.

The same refused transfer in two ordersTwo rows of three boxes show how many clubs Ardi is registered with after each step of a transfer that Riverside refuses. In the top row, labelled release first, the release is refused and the transfer stops, and Ardi stays registered with one club throughout. In the bottom row, labelled register first, Hillside registers him, so he is with two clubs, and then the release is refused, leaving him with two clubs. The last box of the bottom row is highlighted as broken.Release firstRegister firststartrelease: refusedstopstartregisterrelease: refused1 club1 club1 club1 club2 clubs2 clubsA transfer that Riverside refuses. Only one order leaves Ardi with one club.

If you step back, the whole story fits in three sentences, and you could probably have come up with them yourself:

  1. Some rules are about one object, and that object enforces them.
  2. Some rules are about several objects together, and they belong to someone who can see all of them.
  3. That someone asks each object to do its own part, and decides the order, doing the risky step first.

The same shape turns up everywhere once you look for it. A seat on a flight holds at most one passenger, so swapping two passengers' seats is handled by the booking system rather than by either seat. An item in an online game belongs to exactly one player, so trades go through the game server, and online games have had famous bugs where a badly ordered trade duplicated an item.

docs.title: Naming it
docs.text:
These ideas have standard names, and you will meet them in every book on object-oriented design.

Definitions

Responsibility. A job or a rule that a class owns. Deciding which class owns which rule is called assigning responsibilities, and it is a large part of what design means.

Delegation. Asking the object that owns some data to do the work, rather than reaching into that data yourself. The federation delegates "release Ardi" to Riverside.

Invariant. A rule that must be true whenever no operation is in the middle of running. "A player is registered with exactly one club" is an invariant of the whole league, even though for a moment, halfway through a transfer, it may not hold.

docs.title: In our bank
docs.text:
Our bank has exactly this problem, with money in place of players. Ada and Alan each have an account. Ada has 500 euros and tries to send 800 to Alan, using the classes from Module 1 and the most obvious two lines:

Customer ada = new Customer("Ada Lovelace");
Customer alan = new Customer("Alan Turing");

Account from = ada.openAccount(500.00);
Account to = alan.openAccount(2500.00);

// Ada has 500. She tries to send 800.
from.withdraw(800.00);   // returns false, and nobody looked
to.deposit(800.00);      // so this runs anyway

Before: 3000.00 in the two accounts
Account AC-1001: 500.00 EUR
Account AC-1002: 3300.00 EUR
After:  3800.00 in the two accounts

800 euros have appeared from nowhere.

You have seen this story already. withdraw correctly refused, because 800 is more than 500. deposit correctly accepted a positive amount. Each account kept its own rules, and the rule that broke belongs to neither of them: money that leaves one account must arrive in another, and money that arrives must have left somewhere. It is the bank's version of "one player, one club".

So the question from the football story comes back. Who can see both accounts?

Candidate Why it is the wrong owner Account from.transferTo(to, amount) would work for this one rule. But transfers collect rules of their own, such as daily limits, fees and checks between customers, and each would land in a class whose job is to look after one balance. Customer Ada's Customer has no way to reach Alan's account, and Module 1 made sure it never would. main That is where the rule lives now. Code in main cannot be called from anywhere else, cannot be tested, and is replaced when the program gets a window.

None of these can see every account. The bank can: it holds every customer, and through them every account. It plays the role the federation played for the clubs, so the transfer rule goes there.

docs.title: The Bank class
docs.text:
public class Bank {

    private final String name;
    private final List<Customer> customers = new ArrayList<>();

    public Bank(String name) {
        if (name == null || name.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                    "A bank cannot have a blank name.");
        }
        this.name = name.trim();
    }

    // Same shape as openAccount on Customer. The bank makes the customer
    // rather than accepting one, so it can never hold somebody else's.
    public Customer addCustomer(String customerName) {
        Customer customer = new Customer(customerName);
        customers.add(customer);
        return customer;
    }

    public List<Customer> getCustomers() {
        return List.copyOf(customers);
    }

If this looks familiar, it should. It is the pattern you used for Customer in week 4, one level up: a private list created where it is declared, a method that creates the customer rather than accepting one from outside, and a copy handed out instead of the list itself.

A bank owning customers that own accountsA Bank object holds a name and a private customers field. That field points at a list whose two slots point out to two separate Customer objects. Each customer holds its own accounts field, pointing out to one Account object. The same shape repeats at every level: something owns a private list, and the list holds arrows to objects that live outside it.BankBank of TiranacustomersListCustomerCustomerC-1001 AdaC-1002 AlanaccountsaccountsAC-1001AC-1002300.002700.00The same shape at every level. Something owns a private list, and the list holds arrows.

docs.title: Delegation: finding an account by asking
docs.text:
A transfer arrives as two account numbers, so the first job is to find the accounts. The bank does not hold accounts directly, so it does what the federation did: it asks the ones who do.

    public Account findAccount(String accountNumber) {
        for (Customer customer : customers) {
            Account account = customer.findAccount(accountNumber);
            if (account != null) {
                return account;
            }
        }
        return null;
    }

Each customer searches its own accounts with the findAccount method it already had. The bank never opens a customer's list.

docs.title: The transfer
docs.text:
public boolean transfer(String fromNumber, String toNumber,
                            double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                    "A transfer must be positive: " + amount);
        }

        Account from = findAccount(fromNumber);
        Account to = findAccount(toNumber);

        if (from == null || to == null) {
            return false;
        }
        if (from.equals(to)) {
            return false;
        }
        if (!from.withdraw(amount)) {
            return false;
        }
        to.deposit(amount);
        return true;
    }

Look for any arithmetic in this method, or any check on a balance. There is none. Account still does both, exactly as before. What transfer contributes is the order, and the order follows the same reasoning as the football transfer:

  1. A zero or negative amount is a mistake in the code that called the method, so it throws. Nothing has moved.
  2. An account number that does not exist is an ordinary request that cannot be met, so it returns false. Nothing has moved.
  3. A transfer from an account to itself is refused. Nothing has moved.
  4. The withdrawal is the step that can fail, so it runs first. If there is not enough money, it returns false, and nothing has moved.
  5. The deposit runs last. It cannot fail, because stage 1 already rejected every amount that deposit would refuse.

Here is the same picture as before, with money in place of players:

The same failed transfer in two ordersTwo rows of three boxes show the total in the bank after each step of a transfer of 800 from an account holding 500. In the top row, labelled withdraw first, the withdrawal fails and the method stops, and the total stays at 3000 throughout. In the bottom row, labelled deposit first, the deposit raises the total to 3800, the withdrawal then fails, and the method ends with 3800. The last box of the bottom row is highlighted as broken.Withdraw firstDeposit firststartwithdraw: falsereturn falsestartdeposit 800withdraw: false3000.003000.003000.003000.003800.003800.00Sending 800 from an account holding 500. Only one order leaves the total alone.

In the bottom row the method also returns false, so whoever called it believes nothing happened, while 800 euros have appeared in Alan's account.

docs.title: Checking the invariant
docs.text:
An invariant you can calculate is an invariant you can check. The bank adds up what its customers hold every time it is asked:

    public double getTotalDeposits() {
        double total = 0;
        for (Customer customer : customers) {
            total += customer.getTotalBalance();
        }
        return total;
    }

It calculates the total instead of storing it, for the same reason Customer.getTotalBalance does: a stored copy could drift away from the real figure. Now run the same two transfers through the bank. TransferApp prints the total after each one:

boolean tooMuch = bank.transfer(
        from.getAccountNumber(), to.getAccountNumber(), 800.00);
boolean sent = bank.transfer(
        from.getAccountNumber(), to.getAccountNumber(), 200.00);

Total on deposit: 3000.00
Sending 800: false
Total on deposit: 3000.00   (nothing moved)
Sending 200: true
Account AC-1003: 300.00 EUR
Account AC-1004: 2700.00 EUR
Total on deposit: 3000.00   (still the same)

One transfer refused, one accepted, and the total never moves.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Ignoring the answer a method gives you

from.withdraw(800.00);   // compiles, and the false is lost

withdraw returns boolean so that the caller can decide what to do next. Calling it as a statement on its own line throws that answer away, and Java allows it without a warning. If a method reports an outcome, read it.

Reaching into another object's data instead of asking

// Inside Bank. It works, and it is the wrong shape.
for (Customer customer : customers) {
    for (Account account : customer.getAccounts()) {
        if (account.getAccountNumber().equals(accountNumber)) {
            return account;
        }
    }
}

This version makes Bank depend on how a customer stores its accounts and on how account numbers are compared. Change either of those, and you edit two classes instead of one. Asking customer.findAccount(...) keeps that knowledge where it belongs.

docs.title: The bigger picture
docs.text:
Real software runs into this all the time. When you buy something online, one order touches the stock in a warehouse, a payment, and a delivery. None of those three can own the rule "an order is either fully placed or not placed at all", so real systems have a class whose whole job is to coordinate them, often with a name like Checkout or OrderService.

Sometimes the owner already exists in your design, as the bank did here. Sometimes it does not, and you create a class named after the thing that happens: a Transfer, a Booking, an Enrolment. Both follow the same principle.

What if both steps can fail?

The transfer is safe because the deposit cannot fail. That is a property of these two particular operations.

If the receiving account could also refuse, for example because of a maximum balance, no order would be safe on its own. You would need a way to undo the withdrawal when the deposit fails. Java's tools for that need exceptions, which arrive in Module 3, and real banks rely on their database to do it for them.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Some rules belong to one object. Others span several objects, and no single one of them can enforce those.
  • A rule that spans objects belongs to a class that can see all of them. In the bank, that class is Bank.
  • That class delegates: it asks each object to do its own part, and only decides what happens and in which order.
  • Do the step that can fail first, so that a failure leaves nothing to undo.

Key terms: responsibility, delegation, invariant.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Quick checks. Try these before you open the code.

  1. transfer is rewritten with to.deposit(amount) above the withdrawal. Ada has 500. What does sending 800 return, and what is the total afterwards?
  2. bank.transfer(number, number, 50.00), with the same number twice. What does it return, and has any money moved?
  3. bank.transfer(fromNumber, toNumber, -50.00). What happens, and why is it handled differently from question 2?
Answers
  1. It returns false, and the total is 3800. The deposit ran before the withdrawal was refused, so the caller is told nothing happened while 800 euros appeared.
  2. It returns false, and nothing has moved. The check for the same account runs before any money is touched.
  3. It throws IllegalArgumentException. A transfer to yourself is an ordinary request that the bank refuses. A negative amount means the code that called the method has a bug, so it is reported loudly instead.

Coding exercise

Open Bank.transfer, move to.deposit(amount) above the withdrawal, and run TransferApp to check your answer to question 1. Then put it back.

Now add this method to Bank:

public boolean transferWithin(Customer customer, String fromNumber,
                              String toNumber, double amount)

It moves money between two accounts that belong to the same customer. When it works, decide whether it belongs on Bank or on Customer, and write one sentence saying why. Either answer can be defended.

Think about it.

  1. transfer returns false both when an account does not exist and when there is not enough money. For whoever called it, those are different situations. What would have to change if the bank had to report declined transfers grouped by reason?

    Hint

    A boolean can only say yes or no. Count how many different answers the caller needs.

  2. In this week's seminar, a student enrols on a course. That changes the student's list of courses and the course's list of students. Which rules involve both of them, and which class should own those rules?

    Hint

    Ask the question from this page: who can see both the student and the course? If nobody can, that is a class you have not written yet.

Pairs of ideas that look alike and are not

All modules12 pairs

Each pair puts the two ideas side by side, with code from our bank, then states the difference in one or two sentences. Read the question at the bottom of each pair and answer it before you open the answer.

The first two, reference and object, and static and instance, are the ones students mix up most often. Start there.

docs.title: Reference and object
docs.text:
Two references, one objectTwo variables, ada and backup, each hold an arrow. Both arrows point at the same Account object, which holds the number AC-1001 and a balance of 300.00 EUR. There is one account and two references to it.ReferencesObjectadabackupAccountAC-1001300.00 EURAccount backup = ada; copies the arrowstill one account

Reference

The arrow a variable holds. Copying it is cheap and creates nothing.

Account backup = ada;   // a new arrow
vs

Object

The account itself, with its own fields. Only new creates one.

new Account("AC-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 500.00)

The differenceTwo variables can hold arrows to the same object. A change made through either name is a change to that one object.

Check yourselfAccount a = new Account("AC-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 100.00); then Account b = a; and b.deposit(50.00);. What does a.getBalance() return, and how many accounts exist?

150.0, and there is one account. b = a copied the arrow, not the account.

L2.2 What a variable really holds

docs.title: static and instance
Class and object
docs.text:
Class

The description, written once in a .java file.

public class Account { ... }
vs

Object

One thing made from that description while the program runs.

new Account("AC-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 500.00)

The differenceA class is like a blank form, and objects are the filled-in copies: one form, many copies, each with its own answers.

Check yourselfA program declares class Account and calls new Account(...) three times. How many classes and how many objects are there?

One class and three objects.

L2.1 Your first class

docs.title: == and equals
docs.text:
==

For objects, compares references. Are these the same object?

ada == alan   // false: two objects
vs

equals

Compares by the rule the class defines. Do these count as the same thing?

a.equals(b)   // true for two equal Strings

The differenceUse equals for String and for your own classes. For primitives such as int and double, == compares the values themselves.

Check yourselfString a = new String("AC-1001"); and String b = new String("AC-1001");. What do a == b and a.equals(b) give?

false, then true. They are two objects holding the same text.

L2.2 What a variable really holds

docs.title: Field and local variable
docs.text:
Field

Declared in the class, outside every method. It belongs to the object.

private String ownerName;
vs

Local variable

Declared inside a method. It exists only while the method runs.

double total = 0;   // inside getTotalBalance()

The differenceWhen a parameter has the same name as a field, the parameter wins inside the method. this.ownerName reaches the field.

Check yourselfA constructor contains ownerName = ownerName;. It compiles. What does the field hold afterwards?

null. The line assigns the parameter to itself, so the field is never set. Write this.ownerName = ownerName;.

L2.1 Your first class

docs.title: Constructor and method
docs.text:
Constructor

Runs once, through new. Same name as the class, no return type.

public Account(String accountNumber, ...)
vs

Method

Runs each time it is called. Always has a return type, even if void.

public boolean deposit(double amount)

The differenceAdding a return type turns a constructor into a method: public void Account(...) is a method that happens to share the class's name.

Check yourselfThe class has only public void Account(String n, String o, double b). Why does new Account("AC-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 500.00) not compile?

That declaration is a method, not a constructor. The class has no constructor that takes three arguments.

L2.1 Your first class

docs.title: final and immutable
docs.text:
final

The field cannot be pointed at anything else once it has a value.

private final List<Account> accounts
        = new ArrayList<>();
vs

Immutable

The object itself cannot change after it is built.

String name = "ada";   // no method changes it

The differencefinal fixes the arrow; immutable fixes the object. A final list can still have accounts added to it.

Check yourselfWith private final List<Account> accounts, can accounts.add(...) run? Can accounts = new ArrayList<>(); run?

The first, yes: the list itself can change. The second, no: the field is final, so it cannot be pointed at another list.

L3.2 What belongs to whom

docs.title: Returning false and throwing an exception
docs.text:
Return false

An ordinary no, which the caller should expect and handle.

if (!account.withdraw(900.00)) { ... }
vs

Throw

A request that should never have been made, which means a bug in the caller.

throw new IllegalArgumentException(
        "Deposit must be positive: " + amount);

The differenceNot having enough money is a normal answer, so withdraw returns false. A negative amount means the calling code is wrong, so the account throws.

Check yourselfWhich of these should refuse with an exception: withdrawing more than the balance, or creating an account with a null owner name?

The null owner name. Asking for more money than you have is an ordinary request that can simply be answered no.

L3.1 Objects that refuse

docs.title: Array and ArrayList
docs.text:
Array

Fixed length, chosen when it is created. Read it with length.

Account[] accounts = new Account[3];
vs

ArrayList

Grows and shrinks. Read it with size(), change it with add and remove.

List<Account> accounts = new ArrayList<>();

The differenceBoth hold references to objects. Use an array when the size is fixed and known in advance, and a list when items come and go.

Check yourselfaccounts was created with new Account[3], and all three places are used. What happens on accounts[3] = new Account("Grace Hopper", 1500.00);?

An ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The array cannot grow; its valid positions are 0, 1 and 2.

L4.1 Many objects

docs.title: null and empty
docs.text:
null

No object at all. Any method call on it throws a NullPointerException.

List<Account> accounts = null;
vs

Empty

A real object with nothing in it. Its methods work and report zero.

List<Account> accounts = new ArrayList<>();

The differenceReturn an empty list rather than null, so the caller's loop simply runs zero times. For text the same holds: "" is an empty String, and null is no String.

Check yourselfWhat does accounts.isEmpty() give when accounts is null?

Neither true nor false: it throws a NullPointerException, because there is no list to ask.

L4.1 Many objects

docs.title: Overriding and overloading
docs.text:
Overriding

Same name and same parameter types as an inherited method. Your version replaces it.

@Override
public boolean equals(Object other)
vs

Overloading

Same name, different parameter types. A second, separate method.

public boolean equals(Account other)

The differenceList.contains calls equals(Object). It never calls an equals(Account) overload, so the list keeps comparing identity. Writing @Override turns that mistake into a compile error.

Check yourselfA class has @Override above public boolean equals(Account other) and no other equals. What happens?

It does not compile. The method overrides nothing, because Object.equals takes an Object.

L5.2 Object Equality

docs.title: Switch statement and switch expression
docs.text:
Switch statement

Runs code in each branch. It need not cover every case.

switch (choice) {
    case "1" -> listCustomers();
    default -> System.out.println("No such option.");
}
vs

Switch expression

Produces a value. Over an enum it must cover every constant.

boolean allowed = switch (type) {
    case CHECKING -> balance - amount >= 0.00;
    case SAVINGS -> balance - amount >= 100.00;
    case TERM_DEPOSIT -> false;
};

The differenceUse an expression when you are choosing a value. Adding a constant to the enum then turns every forgotten switch into a compile error instead of a silent default.

Check yourselfA switch expression over AccountType covers CHECKING and SAVINGS only. What happens?

It does not compile: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values.

docs.title: Object
docs.text:
A thing in a running program that keeps its own data and offers actions on that data. Each bank account in the program is one object.

Account ada = new Account("AC-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 500.00);
ada.withdraw(200.00);   // ask the object to act

Often confused withClass. The class is the description; objects are made from it, and one class can produce any number of them.

ClassState and behaviourReferenceL1.1 Thinking in things

docs.title: State and behaviour
docs.text:
An object's state is what it knows at this moment, held in its fields. Its behaviour is what it can do, written as its methods.

private double balance;                    // state

public boolean withdraw(double amount) {   // behaviour
    ...

docs.title: Class
docs.text:
A description of one kind of object: which fields every object of that kind has, and which methods it can run. Writing a class creates no objects; new does.

public class Account {

    private String accountNumber;
    private String ownerName;
    private double balance;

    // constructor and methods
}

Often confused withObject. Account is written once; the bank creates thousands of account objects from it.

ObjectConstructorFieldMethodL2.1 Your first class

docs.title: Field
docs.text:
A variable declared inside a class but outside every method. Each object gets its own copy, and it lives as long as the object does.

public class Account {
    private double balance;   // every account has its own
}

Often confused withLocal variable. A local variable is declared inside a method and disappears when the method ends.

State and behaviourEncapsulationfinalL2.1 Your first class

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
Code that runs once, when new creates an object, to give its fields their first values. It has the class's name and no return type.

public Account(String accountNumber, String ownerName,
               double openingBalance) {
    this.accountNumber = accountNumber;
    this.ownerName = ownerName;
    this.balance = openingBalance;
}

Often confused withMethod. A constructor runs once per object, at creation. A method can be called on the object any number of times.

ClassObjectthisL2.1 Your first class

docs.title: this
docs.text:
Inside a constructor or method, this is a reference to the object the code is running on. this.ownerName means this object's field, even when a parameter has the same name.

this.ownerName = ownerName;   // field = parameter

Often confused withLeaving it out. ownerName = ownerName; assigns the parameter to itself, and the field keeps its old value.

ConstructorFieldL2.1 Your first class

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
An action an object can perform, written inside its class. It can read and change the object's fields and can return a result.

public boolean deposit(double amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) {
        return false;
    }
    balance += amount;
    return true;
}

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
What a variable of a class type actually holds: an arrow to an object, not the object itself. Copying the variable copies the arrow, so both names reach the same object.

Account ada = new Account("AC-1001", "Ada Lovelace", 500.00);
Account backup = ada;        // a second arrow, same account
backup.withdraw(200.00);
System.out.println(ada.getBalance());   // 300.0

Often confused withObject. backup = ada creates no new account. Only new creates objects.

ObjectnullPassing an object to a methodL2.2 What a variable really holds

docs.title: null
docs.text:
The value of a reference that points at no object. Calling a method through it throws a NullPointerException.

Account closed = null;
closed.getBalance();   // NullPointerException

Often confused withEmpty. A null list is no list at all. An empty list is a real list with nothing in it.

ReferenceL2.2 What a variable really holds

docs.title: Passing an object to a method
docs.text:
Java copies the value of each argument into the parameter. For an object that value is the reference, so the method works on the caller's object, not on a copy of it.

public static void applyFee(Account account) {
    account.withdraw(5.00);
}

applyFee(ada);   // ada's balance drops by 5

docs.title: Invariant
docs.text:
A rule about an object's state that must hold from the moment it is constructed and after every method call. For an account: the balance is never negative.

if (openingBalance < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException(
            "Opening balance cannot be negative: "
            + openingBalance);
}
EncapsulationConstructorL3.1 Objects that refuse

docs.title: Encapsulation
docs.text:
Keeping an object's fields private, so the only way to change them is through methods that check the change first. The object can then keep its own invariants.

private double balance;

public void deposit(double amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                "Deposit must be positive: " + amount);
    }
    balance += amount;
}

Often confused withPrivate fields with a setter for each. A setter that accepts any value protects nothing.

InvariantGetter and setterFieldL3.1 Objects that refuse

docs.title: Getter and setter
docs.text:
A getter returns a field's value. A setter changes a field, and should refuse values that break the object's rules. Write a setter only for a field that is allowed to change.

public double getBalance() {
    return balance;
}

public void setOwnerName(String ownerName) {
    this.ownerName = requireText(ownerName, "Owner name");
}
EncapsulationL3.1 Objects that refuse

docs.title: final
docs.text:
A final field gets its value once, in the constructor, and can never be reassigned. Use it for facts that do not change, such as an account number.

private final String accountNumber;

Often confused withImmutable. A final field cannot be pointed at another object, but the object it points at can still change.

Immutable objectFieldL3.2 What belongs to whom

docs.title: Immutable object
docs.text:
An object whose state cannot change after it is built: every field is final and there are no setters. String is immutable; its methods return new strings.

String name = "ada lovelace";
name.toUpperCase();          // returns a new String
System.out.println(name);    // ada lovelace
name = name.toUpperCase();   // keep the new one
finalL3.2 What belongs to whom

docs.title: static
docs.text:
A static field or method belongs to the class itself, not to any object. There is one copy, shared by every object, and you reach it through the class name.

private static int lastNumberIssued = 1000;   // one for all

Account.getAccountsOpened();   // called on the class

Often confused withInstance fields. Every object has its own balance; there is only one lastNumberIssued.

docs.title: List and ArrayList
docs.text:
List describes what an ordered collection can do; ArrayList is a class that does it, and it grows as you add items. A list holds references to objects, not copies of them.

List<Account> accounts = new ArrayList<>();
accounts.add(new Account("Ada Lovelace", 500.00));
accounts.get(0);    // the first account
accounts.size();    // how many there are

Often confused withArray. An array's length is fixed when it is created. A list grows and shrinks.

Referencefor-each loopHas-a relationshipL4.1 Many objects

docs.title: for-each loop
docs.text:
A loop that visits every element of a collection in order, without an index. The loop variable holds each reference in turn, so you can call methods on the objects but cannot replace them in the list.

for (Account account : accounts) {
    account.deposit(10.00);   // every account gains 10
}
List and ArrayListL4.1 Many objects

docs.title: Has-a relationship
docs.text:
One object keeps others in its fields and is responsible for them. A customer has accounts: it opens them, finds them and totals them, and no other class changes its list.

public class Customer {

    private final List<Account> accounts = new ArrayList<>();

    public Account openAccount(double openingBalance) {
        ...
    }
}

Often confused withIs-a, the relationship behind inheritance, which you meet in week 7. A customer has accounts; a customer is not an account.

docs.title: Defensive copy
docs.text:
Returning a copy of an internal list instead of the list itself, so the caller can read it but cannot add or remove items behind the owner's back.

public List<Account> getAccounts() {
    return List.copyOf(accounts);
}
