docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
A job or a rule that a class owns. Deciding which class owns which rule is called assigning responsibilities. The usual answer is the class that holds the information needed to decide.

// Bank holds every customer, so Bank owns the transfer rule.
public boolean transfer(String fromNumber, String toNumber,
                        double amount) {
    ...
}
DelegationSingle Responsibility PrincipleL5.1 Object Collaboration

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
Asking the object that owns some data to do the work, instead of reaching into that data yourself.

// Bank asks each customer. It never loops over their accounts.
for (Customer customer : customers) {
    Account account = customer.findAccount(accountNumber);
    if (account != null) {
        return account;
    }
}
return null;

Often confused withReaching in. Calling customer.getAccounts() and looping in Bank works, and it puts the customer's job in the wrong class.

ResponsibilityHas-a relationshipL5.1 Object Collaboration

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Two references point to the very same object. In Java, == tests identity.

Account restored = new Account(number, 500.00);
System.out.println(account == restored);   // false

Often confused withEquality. Two objects can be equal by the class's rule and still be two separate objects.

EqualityReferenceL5.2 Object Equality

docs.title: Equality
docs.text:
Two objects count as the same thing according to a rule the class defines in its equals method. A class that does not override equals falls back to identity.

@Override
public boolean equals(Object other) {
    if (this == other) {
        return true;
    }
    if (!(other instanceof Account)) {
        return false;
    }
    Account that = (Account) other;
    return accountNumber.equals(that.accountNumber);
}
IdentityValue and entityhashCode and its contractL5.2 Object Equality

docs.title: Value and entity
docs.text:
A value is equal to another when all its parts match, like an amount of money. An entity is equal to another when its identifier matches, like an account and its account number.

// Account is an entity: only the number decides.
return accountNumber.equals(that.accountNumber);
EqualityL5.2 Object Equality

docs.title: hashCode and its contract
docs.text:
hashCode returns a number that collections such as HashSet and HashMap use to choose a group, called a bucket, for each object. The contract: objects that are equal must have equal hash codes, so override both methods or neither.

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(accountNumber);
}

Often confused withEquality. Equal hash codes do not make two objects equal. Different accounts may share a hash code.

docs.title: Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
A class should have one reason to change: one person, or one kind of request, can ask for a change to it. Named by Robert C. Martin; the S in SOLID.

// Account, Customer, Bank: the rules about money change
// BankConsole: the wording or the menu changes
// ConsoleApp:  the way the program is put together changes
ResponsibilitySeparation of concernsModel and user interfaceL6.1 The Single Responsibility Principle

docs.title: Separation of concerns
docs.text:
Keeping code for different concerns, such as rules, presentation and storage, in different places, so that a change to one does not disturb the others.

Bank bank = new Bank("Bank of Tirana");       // the rules
BankConsole console = new BankConsole(bank, input);
console.run();                                // the talking
Single Responsibility PrincipleModel and user interfaceL6.1 The Single Responsibility Principle

docs.title: Model and user interface
docs.text:
The model holds the data and enforces the rules; it never reads input or prints. The user interface talks to people and turns their requests into method calls on the model.

// The console asks, the bank decides, the console reports.
if (bank.transfer(from, to, amount)) {
    System.out.printf("Sent %.2f EUR.%n", amount);
} else {
    System.out.println("That transfer did not go through.");
}
Separation of concernsSingle Responsibility PrincipleL6.1 The Single Responsibility Principle

docs.title: Enumeration (enum)
docs.text:
A type with a fixed set of values, listed once in its declaration. No value outside the list can exist.

public enum AccountType {

    CHECKING,
    SAVINGS,
    TERM_DEPOSIT
}

Often confused withA set of String constants. The compiler cannot check text: "CHEKING" compiles.

Enum constantType safetySwitch expressionL6.2 Enumerations

docs.title: Enum constant
docs.text:
One value of an enum, such as AccountType.SAVINGS. Each constant is an object created once when the program starts, so it can hold fields and answer method calls.

SAVINGS("Savings account", 0.0025),

AccountType.SAVINGS.getMonthlyInterestRate();   // 0.0025
Enumeration (enum)values() and valueOf()L6.2 Enumerations

docs.title: Type safety
docs.text:
The compiler's guarantee that a variable holds only values of its declared type. An AccountType variable holds one of the three constants, or null, and nothing else.

AccountType type = AccountType.CHEKING;   // does not compile
Enumeration (enum)L6.2 Enumerations

docs.title: Switch expression
docs.text:
A switch that produces a value. Over an enum, the compiler checks that every constant is covered, so adding a constant points you at every switch you need to update.

boolean allowed = switch (type) {
    case CHECKING -> balance - amount >= 0.00;
    case SAVINGS -> balance - amount >= 100.00;
    case TERM_DEPOSIT -> false;
};

Often confused withThe switch statement, which runs code instead of producing a value and needs a default branch to compile in cases like this one.

Enumeration (enum)Enum constantL6.2 Enumerations

docs.title: values() and valueOf()
docs.text:
Methods every enum has without writing them. values() returns all the constants in declaration order; valueOf turns text into a constant and throws an exception for text it does not recognise.

for (AccountType type : AccountType.values()) {
    System.out.println(type.getLabel());
}
AccountType.valueOf("CRYPTO");   // IllegalArgumentException

docs.title: The Project
docs.text:
One application, one team, two sprints

Teams of 2 to 4Sprint 1 · 10 pointsSprint 2 · 20 pointsSprint 1 demos 14 to 18 December

In the lectures you watch a bank being built. In the seminars you build a university system that someone else designed. The project is where you decide everything yourselves: what the program is for, which classes it needs, and how they work together.

You build one application with the same team for the whole semester. Sprint 1 turns it into a working console program using Modules 1 and 2. Sprint 2 takes the same code and finishes it with Modules 3 and 4. You never start over.

docs.title: The timeline
docs.text:
• Now. Form a team of two to four people and choose an idea from the project ideas, or bring your own.
  • Friday 4 December, 23:59. Your project card is in your repository, and the repository link is submitted.
  • Week of 7 December. Feedback on your card in the seminar. Build.
  • Sunday 13 December, 23:59. The Sprint 1 version is tagged sprint-1 in your repository.
  • 14 to 18 December. Sprint 1 demos, in the lecture and seminar sessions.
  • End of the semester. Sprint 2 demos. The date is announced in class.

docs.title: The two sprints
docs.text:
• Sprint 1 · 10 points

    A console program built from classes you designed: objects that protect their own state, a class hierarchy, collections, an enum, and a menu kept apart from the rules.

    Covers Modules 1 and 2.

    Read the brief

  • Sprint 2 · 20 points

    The same program, finished. It survives bad input, saves its data, has tests that prove it works, and gets a window on top.

    Covers Modules 3 and 4. The brief opens after Sprint 1.

docs.title: Choosing what to build
docs.text:
The project ideas page has ten ideas with a suggested design for each. You can take one as it is, change it, or propose something of your own that meets the same checklist.

Two domains are not allowed: a bank, because that is the lecture application, and a university system, because that is the seminar one. Using an idea in a domain you have not seen yet is the part that teaches you something.

Keep the idea small enough to finish. A program with five classes that all work is worth more than a plan for fifteen.

docs.title: Your repository
docs.text:
• One GitHub repository per team. One member creates it and adds the others as collaborators.
  • Every member commits their own work, from their own account, throughout the sprint. The history shows who built what.
  • The README says what the program does, how to run it, and how you used AI tools.
  • Each sprint is submitted by tagging a commit. The Sprint 1 brief shows how.

docs.title: Using AI tools
docs.text:
You may use AI tools: to explain an error, to compare two designs, or to write code. You own what you hand in. At the demo, every member must be able to explain any part of the program and change it while we watch.

State in your README which tools you used and what you used them for. Work that nobody in the team can explain is graded as work the team did not do.

docs.title: How you are graded
docs.text:
Each sprint is graded in four areas. Three of them look at the code and the repository, and every member of the team gets the same marks for them. The fourth is the demo, where each person answers questions on their own, so it is graded per person. The demo carries the most weight.

If the commit history shows that one member did very little, their marks for the team areas can be lowered as well.

docs.title: Your own idea
docs.text:
You can build something that is not on this page. Check it against this list before you write the project card. If it ticks every box, it is big enough for Sprint 1 and has room for Sprint 2.

  • Someone would actually use it, and you can say who in one sentence
  • At least four classes of your own, not counting the console class and main
  • An abstract class with at least two subclasses that behave differently, not only hold different data
  • One class that owns a list of other objects and does the work on that list
  • An enum whose constants carry at least one value each
  • At least four menu actions that change something or report something
  • Not a bank and not a university system
  • Something obvious to add in Sprint 2: saving, a rule that can fail, a window

Project card

docs.title: Project card
docs.text:
One page, before any code

One per teamDue Friday 4 December, 23:59

The project card is your plan on one page: who is in the team, what the program is for, which classes it needs, and who builds what first. Writing it takes an hour. It is much cheaper to fix a weak design on one page than in five hundred lines of code.

You get feedback on your card in the seminar the week after you submit it.

docs.title: How to submit
docs.text:
1. One member creates the team's GitHub repository and adds the others as collaborators.
  2. Copy the template below into a file called PROJECT_CARD.md at the top of the repository, fill it in, then commit and push it.
  3. Submit the repository link by Friday 4 December, 23:59.

The card stays in the repository. If your plan changes during the sprint, update the card and say what changed and why.

Turing Wheels, a car rental

Team: Turing Wheels. Ada Lovelace (ada-l), Alan Turing (aturing), Grace Hopper (ghopper).

The idea. A small agency rents cars, vans and scooters by the day. Staff use the program to see what is available, rent a vehicle to a customer, and take it back.

Class What it is responsible for Agency Keeps the fleet and the customers, and decides whether a rental can go ahead Customer Keeps their contact details and their rentals, past and current Vehicle Keeps its plate and state, and works out the price for a number of days Rental Records which vehicle, which customer, how many days, and the price

docs.title: What makes a good card
docs.text:
• The idea fits in two sentences. If it needs a paragraph, it is probably two programs.
  • Each class has one responsibility, and you can say it in one short sentence. "Keeps the vehicles and prints the menu" mixes the rules with the talking, so it is two classes.
  • The subclasses behave differently. If Car and Van differ only in a field value, an enum is the better design, and you still need a real hierarchy somewhere else.
  • The work is split by class, not by "Ada writes the code, Alan writes the README". Everyone writes Java.

Sprint 1

docs.title: Sprint 1
docs.text:
Your own program, built from Modules 1 and 2

10 pointsTeams of 2 to 4Tag by Sunday 13 December, 23:59Demos 14 to 18 December

What you will hand in

  • A console program that does something useful, built from classes your team designed
  • A repository with a README, a class diagram and commits from every member
  • A demo where each of you explains the code and changes it live

docs.title: What you build
docs.text:
A program that runs in the console and manages the objects of your idea: it creates them, connects them, changes them through a menu, and reports on them. The rules live in your model classes, and the menu only asks and reports, the way Bank and BankConsole divide the work in the week 6 code.

Everything you need was covered in Modules 1 and 2. The links in the list below go to the matching cards on the Key Concepts pages, so the list doubles as a revision guide.

docs.title: Classes that protect their state
docs.text:
• At least four classes of your own, not counting the console class and main
  • Every field is private, and final where it never changes
  • Constructors refuse invalid values, so no object can exist in a broken state (invariant, encapsulation)
  • Setters only for fields that are allowed to change, and they check the new value too (getter and setter)

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• One inheritance hierarchy: an abstract class with at least two subclasses (weeks 7 and 8)
  • At least one method that each subclass overrides, called in a loop over a list of the parent type, with no instanceof deciding what to do
  • One class that owns a list of other objects and never hands that list out (has-a relationship, defensive copy)
  • Work done by the class that owns the data, not by a class that reaches into it (responsibility, delegation)

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• Your objects kept in a List and worked through with loops (List, for-each)
  • An enum whose constants carry at least one value each (enum constant)
  • equals and hashCode for one class whose objects are identified by a code or a number (equality, hashCode)

docs.title: The console
docs.text:
• A menu that repeats until the user chooses to quit
  • Wrong input, such as a letter where a number belongs or an option that does not exist, gets a message instead of a crash. Read every answer with nextLine() and convert it the way BankConsole does in the week 6 code
  • Only the console class reads input and prints. The model classes contain no System.out (model and user interface)
  • Sample data created when the program starts, so there is something to show straight away. The course uses Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing and Grace Hopper; you may too

docs.title: The repository
docs.text:
• A README with what the program does, how to run it, the menu, a class diagram, and how you used AI tools
  • Commits from every member, spread across the sprint rather than all on the last night
  • The version you submit tagged sprint-1

For a stronger project

None of these are required. Each one shows that you can choose a design, not only follow a list.

  • An interface implemented by two classes that are not related by inheritance
  • A place where you held another object instead of inheriting from it, with the reason in your README
  • A switch expression over your enum (switch expression)
  • A rule that needs two objects to agree, such as a transfer between two clubs, owned by the class that holds both

Not in Sprint 1

Exceptions of your own, reading and writing files, tests, and a window all belong to Modules 3 and 4, so they belong to Sprint 2. Keep Sprint 1 to what the requirements ask, and make it work well.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
Ten points in four areas. The first three are team marks: every member gets the same. The demo is marked for each person on their own, and it carries the most weight.

Area Points Full marks look like Points are lost for Design 3 Classes with one clear job each. A hierarchy whose subclasses behave differently. A class that owns its list and does the work on it. Objects that cannot be put into a broken state. Public fields. Subclasses that differ only in data. Lists handed out to be changed. Rules checked in the console instead of the model. Working program 2 Every menu action works. Wrong input gets a message. The model never prints. It runs from the README instructions on a fresh clone. Crashes on bad input. Menu options that do nothing. System.out in model classes. Repository 1 A README with the class diagram and an honest note on AI use. Commits from every member across the sprint. The sprint-1 tag. No class diagram or AI note. One member's commits only. No tag. Demo and answers 4 Marked per person. You explain any part of the program, including parts you did not write, and make a small change while we watch. Not being able to explain code you handed in, whoever or whatever wrote it.

The demo marks for each person:

Points What it looks like 4 Explains clearly why the code is the way it is, and makes the change without help 3 Explains the code correctly, and makes the change with a hint 2 Explains their own part, but not how it connects to the rest 1 Describes what the program does, but not how the code does it 0 Cannot explain the code they handed in

docs.title: The demo
docs.text:
About twelve minutes per team, in your usual lecture or seminar session during the week of 14 December. The schedule is announced in class.

  1. Run it, three minutes. Show three menu actions of your choice and one piece of wrong input.
  2. The design, two minutes. Open your class diagram and say what each class is responsible for.
  3. Questions, about two minutes each. Each member is asked about a part of the code they did not write, then makes one small change, such as adding a constant to the enum or a check to a method, and runs the program again.

Bring the program open in Eclipse on one laptop, ready to run.

docs.title: Submitting
docs.text:
Commit and push your final version, then tag it:

git tag sprint-1
git push origin sprint-1

The tag marks exactly what is graded. Commits after the tag do not count for Sprint 1, so you can keep working on Sprint 2 without worrying. If you tag too early, delete the tag and tag again before the deadline:

git tag -d sprint-1
git push origin --delete sprint-1

docs.title: Before you submit
docs.text:
• A fresh clone runs by following only your README
  • Every menu option works, and typing a letter where a number belongs does not crash it
  • Searching the model classes for System.out finds nothing
  • Every member can explain every class
  • The README states how you used AI tools
  • git tag lists sprint-1, and the tag is on GitHub

Most lost points come from a handful of mix-ups: a reference and an object, static and instance, == and equals. Read those three pairs again before the demo.
